**Taunton Castle** is a [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") built to defend the town of [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton "Taunton"), [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset"), England. It has origins in the [Anglo Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") period and was later the site of a [priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priory "Priory"). The [Normans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") then built a [stone structured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_architecture "Norman architecture") castle, which belonged to the [Bishops of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"). The current heavily reconstructed buildings are the inner ward, which now houses the [Museum of Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Somerset "Museum of Somerset") and the [Somerset Military Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Military_Museum "Somerset Military Museum"). The building was designated a grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") in 1952.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-1)

## Anglo Saxon origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Anglo Saxon origins")]

The earliest fortification of Taunton started for King [Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex "Ine of Wessex") and [Æthelburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelburg_of_Wessex "Æthelburg of Wessex"), in or about the year 710. However, according to the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_ this was destroyed twelve years later,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) however it is unlikely this was on the site of the current castle.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3) An ecclesiastical [minster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minster_(church) "Minster (church)") is traditionally said to have been founded at Taunton, only a few years later, by Queen [Frithugyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frithugyth "Frithugyth"), wife of King [Æthelheard of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelheard_of_Wessex "Æthelheard of Wessex"), and the Bishops of Wessex appear to have built a manor house, adjoining it.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2)

## Medieval and Tudor eras

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Medieval and Tudor eras")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_%281897%29.jpg/330px-Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_%281897%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_(1897).jpg)

A plan of the castle from J. D. Mackenzie's _The Castles of England: their story and structure_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-4)

At the time of the [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book") in 1086, Taunton belonged to the [Bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"), who had a minster or [Augustinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustinians "Augustinians")[Priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priory "Priory") on the site. Between 1107 and 1129 [William Giffard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Giffard "William Giffard"), the Chancellor of King [Henry I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I_of_England "Henry I of England"), converted the bishop's hall into a castle. In 1216, Bishop [Peter des Roches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_des_Roches "Peter des Roches"), a supporter of King John, defended the castle during a barons' revolt.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) By the late 12th century the [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") measured 65 feet (20 m) by 98 feet (30 m) with a first floor great hall over a stone vaulted undercroft. During the [Second Barons' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Barons'_War "Second Barons' War") it was used as a prison for the son of [Simon de Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester "Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester") who was held here until 1282. In 1451, when the [Earl of Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Devon "Earl of Devon") besieged the castle which was held by [Lord Bonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bonville,_1st_Baron_Bonville "William Bonville, 1st Baron Bonville"), it was arranged around two baileys.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3)

The gate-house of the inner ward was probably of [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England")'s date (1239–1307), but it was changed by Bishop [Walter Langton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Langton "Walter Langton") in 1496.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) He inserted a large two-lighted [Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_period "Tudor period") window and placed a tablet bearing his own arms, supported by angels, above it and the Royal Coat of King [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") below. The Great Hall, which stands just opposite the gateway, is 120 feet (37 m) by 31 feet (9 m), with walls apparently, in part, Norman, but much changed by later generations. Bishop Langton inserted Tudor windows but all of them, save two in the north front, have been replaced by seventeenth- or eighteenth-century substitutes. The last building erected within the walls was a schoolhouse, paid for by Bishop [Richard Foxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Foxe "Richard Foxe") in the 1520s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3)

## Stuart era and Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Stuart era and Civil War")]

Taunton Castle had fallen into ruin by 1600 but it was repaired during the Civil War. Taunton had been captured by the Parliamentarian army under the [Earl of Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Devereux,_3rd_Earl_of_Essex "Robert Devereux, 3rd Earl of Essex") in June 1644 making it the only Parliamentary [enclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave "Enclave") in the South West of the country. After Essex's army was forced to surrender at [Lostwithiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lostwithiel "Battle of Lostwithiel") in [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall") in September, the Royalists maintained a [Siege of Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Taunton "Siege of Taunton"). From July 1644 to July 1645 Parliamentary forces commanded by Colonel [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake_(admiral) "Robert Blake (admiral)") were besieged by Royalist forces under [Lord Goring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Goring,_Lord_Goring "George Goring, Lord Goring"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-6) although the town was briefly relieved by [Sir William Waller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Waller "William Waller") in late November.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-8) A relief column under Colonel Ralph Weldon made it to Taunton on 11 May, but the combined forces were still besieged. The two generals held out until help arrived on 14 June after the troops could be spared from the [Battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-9)

It was in the Great Hall, in 1685, that [Judge Jeffreys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jeffreys,_1st_Baron_Jeffreys "George Jeffreys, 1st Baron Jeffreys") held the [Bloody Assizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Assizes "Bloody Assizes") following the [Monmouth Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouth_Rebellion "Monmouth Rebellion").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) Of more than 500 supporters of [James Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Scott,_1st_Duke_of_Monmouth "James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth") brought before the court on 18 and 19 September, 144 were hanged and their remains displayed around the county to ensure people understood the fate of those who rebelled against the king.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-12)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Taunton_Castle2.JPG/250px-Taunton_Castle2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taunton_Castle2.JPG)

Rear of the castle

Taunton was a typical [Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") keep of the first half of the twelfth century, 50 feet (15 m) long by 40 feet (12 m) wide,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) in three stories, with walls some 13 feet (4 m) thick. This was let into the walls of an inner ward with a stone [enceinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceinte "Enceinte") and, there was an [outer bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_bailey "Outer bailey") represented by the modern "Castle Green". Until the late 17th century the castle was still used as a prison.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-pastscape-13)

By 1780, many parts of the castle had fallen into a bad condition and were repaired in a [Georgian style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_architecture "Georgian architecture") by Sir [Benjamin Hammet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Hammet "Benjamin Hammet"), a banker of [Lombard Street, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street,_London "Lombard Street, London"), and the [Member of Parliament for Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Taunton (UK Parliament constituency)"). In 1786 he purchased the grant as bailiff and keeper of Taunton Castle in the names of his sons and his nephew.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-14) He put on a new roof, inserted many windows and recast many other details all round the castle. During the 18th and 19th centuries the Great Hall was used for public meetings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-pastscape-13)

The outer ward is now occupied by two hotels, which have been [crenellated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenellated "Crenellated"), in order to be in keeping with the genuine battlements of the inner ward. But the great gate, opening into the enclosure, where they stand, is in part a genuine antique, having the arches of an "Early Decorated " gate-house of about the time of [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England"), though the superstructure is a restoration of 1816.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) In 1873 it was bought by the [Somerset Archaeological and Natural History Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Archaeological_and_Natural_History_Society "Somerset Archaeological and Natural History Society") and between 1899 and 1900 the Great Hall was repaired and refitted as their chief museum space.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-15) In 1908–9 the Adam Library was created to house the society's growing collection of books.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-16)

## Modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern era")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Taunton_Castle.JPG/250px-Taunton_Castle.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taunton_Castle.JPG)

The closed entrance

The great hall and inner ward of the original castle make up the [Museum of Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Somerset "Museum of Somerset") which opened in September 2011 after a £7 million refurbishment, partially funded by the [Heritage Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-17)

The 17th-century Castle House has been designated as an [Ancient Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Monument "Ancient Monument").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-18) Due to its condition it was placed on the [Heritage at Risk Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_at_Risk_Register "Heritage at Risk Register") and underwent necessary repairs, but as of 2013 is still unoccupied.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-19)

**Taunton Castle** is a [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") built to defend the town of [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton "Taunton"), [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset"), England. It has origins in the [Anglo Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") period and was later the site of a [priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priory "Priory"). The [Normans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") then built a [stone structured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_architecture "Norman architecture") castle, which belonged to the [Bishops of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"). The current heavily reconstructed buildings are the inner ward, which now houses the [Museum of Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Somerset "Museum of Somerset") and the [Somerset Military Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Military_Museum "Somerset Military Museum"). The building was designated a grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") in 1952.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-1)

## Anglo Saxon origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Anglo Saxon origins")]

The earliest fortification of Taunton started for King [Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex "Ine of Wessex") and [Æthelburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelburg_of_Wessex "Æthelburg of Wessex"), in or about the year 710. However, according to the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon\_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_ this was destroyed twelve years later,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) however it is unlikely this was on the site of the current castle.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3) An ecclesiastical [minster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minster_(church) "Minster (church)") is traditionally said to have been founded at Taunton, only a few years later, by Queen [Frithugyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frithugyth "Frithugyth"), wife of King [Æthelheard of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelheard_of_Wessex "Æthelheard of Wessex"), and the Bishops of Wessex appear to have built a manor house, adjoining it.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2)

## Medieval and Tudor eras

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Medieval and Tudor eras")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_%281897%29.jpg/330px-Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_%281897%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_of_Taunton_Castle_(1897).jpg)

A plan of the castle from J. D. Mackenzie's _The Castles of England: their story and structure_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-4)

At the time of the [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book") in 1086, Taunton belonged to the [Bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester"), who had a minster or [Augustinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustinians "Augustinians")[Priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priory "Priory") on the site. Between 1107 and 1129 [William Giffard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Giffard "William Giffard"), the Chancellor of King [Henry I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I_of_England "Henry I of England"), converted the bishop's hall into a castle. In 1216, Bishop [Peter des Roches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_des_Roches "Peter des Roches"), a supporter of King John, defended the castle during a barons' revolt.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) By the late 12th century the [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") measured 65 feet (20 m) by 98 feet (30 m) with a first floor great hall over a stone vaulted undercroft. During the [Second Barons' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Barons'_War "Second Barons' War") it was used as a prison for the son of [Simon de Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_de_Montfort,_6th_Earl_of_Leicester "Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester") who was held here until 1282. In 1451, when the [Earl of Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Devon "Earl of Devon") besieged the castle which was held by [Lord Bonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bonville,_1st_Baron_Bonville "William Bonville, 1st Baron Bonville"), it was arranged around two baileys.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3)

The gate-house of the inner ward was probably of [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England")'s date (1239–1307), but it was changed by Bishop [Walter Langton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Langton "Walter Langton") in 1496.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) He inserted a large two-lighted [Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_period "Tudor period") window and placed a tablet bearing his own arms, supported by angels, above it and the Royal Coat of King [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") below. The Great Hall, which stands just opposite the gateway, is 120 feet (37 m) by 31 feet (9 m), with walls apparently, in part, Norman, but much changed by later generations. Bishop Langton inserted Tudor windows but all of them, save two in the north front, have been replaced by seventeenth- or eighteenth-century substitutes. The last building erected within the walls was a schoolhouse, paid for by Bishop [Richard Foxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Foxe "Richard Foxe") in the 1520s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-dunning-3)

## Stuart era and Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Stuart era and Civil War")]

Taunton Castle had fallen into ruin by 1600 but it was repaired during the Civil War. Taunton had been captured by the Parliamentarian army under the [Earl of Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Devereux,_3rd_Earl_of_Essex "Robert Devereux, 3rd Earl of Essex") in June 1644 making it the only Parliamentary [enclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave "Enclave") in the South West of the country. After Essex's army was forced to surrender at [Lostwithiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lostwithiel "Battle of Lostwithiel") in [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall") in September, the Royalists maintained a [Siege of Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Taunton "Siege of Taunton"). From July 1644 to July 1645 Parliamentary forces commanded by Colonel [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake_(admiral) "Robert Blake (admiral)") were besieged by Royalist forces under [Lord Goring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Goring,_Lord_Goring "George Goring, Lord Goring"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-6) although the town was briefly relieved by [Sir William Waller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Waller "William Waller") in late November.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-8) A relief column under Colonel Ralph Weldon made it to Taunton on 11 May, but the combined forces were still besieged. The two generals held out until help arrived on 14 June after the troops could be spared from the [Battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-9)

It was in the Great Hall, in 1685, that [Judge Jeffreys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jeffreys,_1st_Baron_Jeffreys "George Jeffreys, 1st Baron Jeffreys") held the [Bloody Assizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Assizes "Bloody Assizes") following the [Monmouth Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouth_Rebellion "Monmouth Rebellion").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5) Of more than 500 supporters of [James Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Scott,_1st_Duke_of_Monmouth "James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth") brought before the court on 18 and 19 September, 144 were hanged and their remains displayed around the county to ensure people understood the fate of those who rebelled against the king.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-exmoor-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-12)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Taunton_Castle2.JPG/250px-Taunton_Castle2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taunton_Castle2.JPG)

Rear of the castle

Taunton was a typical [Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") keep of the first half of the twelfth century, 50 feet (15 m) long by 40 feet (12 m) wide,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) in three stories, with walls some 13 feet (4 m) thick. This was let into the walls of an inner ward with a stone [enceinte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceinte "Enceinte") and, there was an [outer bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_bailey "Outer bailey") represented by the modern "Castle Green". Until the late 17th century the castle was still used as a prison.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-pastscape-13)

By 1780, many parts of the castle had fallen into a bad condition and were repaired in a [Georgian style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_architecture "Georgian architecture") by Sir [Benjamin Hammet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Hammet "Benjamin Hammet"), a banker of [Lombard Street, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street,_London "Lombard Street, London"), and the [Member of Parliament for Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Taunton (UK Parliament constituency)"). In 1786 he purchased the grant as bailiff and keeper of Taunton Castle in the names of his sons and his nephew.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-14) He put on a new roof, inserted many windows and recast many other details all round the castle. During the 18th and 19th centuries the Great Hall was used for public meetings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-pastscape-13)

The outer ward is now occupied by two hotels, which have been [crenellated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenellated "Crenellated"), in order to be in keeping with the genuine battlements of the inner ward. But the great gate, opening into the enclosure, where they stand, is in part a genuine antique, having the arches of an "Early Decorated " gate-house of about the time of [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England"), though the superstructure is a restoration of 1816.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-britannia-2) In 1873 it was bought by the [Somerset Archaeological and Natural History Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Archaeological_and_Natural_History_Society "Somerset Archaeological and Natural History Society") and between 1899 and 1900 the Great Hall was repaired and refitted as their chief museum space.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-15) In 1908–9 the Adam Library was created to house the society's growing collection of books.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-16)

## Modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taunton_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern era")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Taunton_Castle.JPG/250px-Taunton_Castle.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taunton_Castle.JPG)

The closed entrance

The great hall and inner ward of the original castle make up the [Museum of Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Somerset "Museum of Somerset") which opened in September 2011 after a £7 million refurbishment, partially funded by the [Heritage Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-17)

The 17th-century Castle House has been designated as an [Ancient Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Monument "Ancient Monument").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-18) Due to its condition it was placed on the [Heritage at Risk Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_at_Risk_Register "Heritage at Risk Register") and underwent necessary repairs, but as of 2013 is still unoccupied.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Castle#cite_note-19)

**Raglan Castle** ([Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language"): _Castell Rhaglan_)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Cadw_name-1) is a [late medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages")[castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") located just north of the village of [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") in the county of [Monmouthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouthshire "Monmouthshire") in south east [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"). The modern castle dates from between the 15th and early 17th centuries, when the successive ruling families of the [Herberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Herbert "Baron Herbert") and the [Somersets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Beaufort "Duke of Beaufort") created a luxurious, fortified castle, complete with a large hexagonal [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep"), known as the Great Tower or the Yellow Tower of [Gwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Gwent "Kingdom of Gwent"). Surrounded by [parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park"), [water gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_garden "Water garden") and [terraces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_garden "Terrace garden"), the castle was considered by contemporaries to be the equal of any other in England or Wales.

During the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"), Raglan was occupied by a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") garrison on behalf of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") but was taken by [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") forces in 1646 and its walls [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting"), or deliberately put beyond military use. After the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in 1660, the Somersets declined to restore it and it became first a source of local building materials, then a [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") ruin. It is now a [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction").

### Early history of the castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history of the castle")]

Following the [Norman invasion of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_invasion_of_Wales "Norman invasion of Wales"), the area around the village of [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") was granted to [William FitzOsbern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_FitzOsbern,_1st_Earl_of_Hereford "William FitzOsbern, 1st Earl of Hereford"), the [Earl of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Hereford "Earl of Hereford").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P3-4) Some historians, such as John Kenyon, suspect that an early [motte and bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motte_and_bailey "Motte and bailey") castle may have been built on the Raglan site during this period: the location had strategic importance and archaeologists have discovered the remains of a possible bailey ditch on the site.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P3-4) The local manor was held by the Bloet family from the late 12th century until the late 14th century, and the family built a manor house somewhere on the site during this period, surrounded by a park.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-5) By the late medieval period the Raglan site was surrounded by the large [deer parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park") of Home Park and Red Deer Park, the latter being enclosed at the end of the period.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6)

### 15th to 16th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 15th to 16th centuries")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg/250px-Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg)

Reconstruction of Raglan Castle around 1620

The current Raglan Castle was begun by [Sir William ap Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_ap_Thomas "William ap Thomas"), the lesser son of a minor Welsh family who rose through the ranks of mid-15th century politics, profiting from the benefits of the local offices he held.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-7) William married first Elizabeth, a wealthy heiress, and then Gwladus, another heiress who would prove to be a powerful regional figure in her own right.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-8) In 1432, [Sir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir "Sir") William purchased the manor of Raglan, where he had already been staying as a tenant, for 1,000 [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_(money) "Mark (money)") (£666 13s 4d) and commenced a programme of building work that established the basic shape of the castle as seen today, although most of it—with the exception of the South Gate and the Great Tower—was later built over.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-11)

Sir William's son dropped the Welsh version of his name, calling himself [William Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herbert,_1st_Earl_of_Pembroke_(1423%E2%80%931469) "William Herbert, 1st Earl of Pembroke (1423–1469)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9) He continued to rise in prominence, supporting the [House of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York") during the [War of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Roses "War of the Roses"), fighting in the [Hundred Years War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years_War "Hundred Years War") in France but making his fortune from the [Gascon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") wine trade.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-12) He was also closely associated with Welsh politics and status; he was the first Welshman to be made an earl and was described by contemporary poets as the "national deliverer" who might achieve Welsh independence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-13) In the 1460s William used his increasing wealth to remodel Raglan on a much grander scale.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-14) The symbolism of the castle architecture may have reflected the Welsh family roots: historian Matthew Johnson has suggested that the polygonal towers were possibly designed to imitate those of [Caernarfon Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caernarfon_Castle "Caernarfon Castle"), whose architecture carries numerous allusions to the eventual return of a Roman Emperor to Wales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-15) Historian Anthony Emery has described the resulting castle as one of the "last formidable displays of medieval defensive architecture".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-16)

There was an important link between Raglan Castle and the surrounding [parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park"), in particular the Home Park and the Red Deer Park.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6) Historian Robert Liddiard suggests that on the basis of the views from the castle at this time, the structured nature of the parks would have contrasted with the wilderness of the mountain peaks framing the scene beyond, making an important statement about the refinement and cultured nature of the castle lord.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-17) In the 15th century there were also extensive orchards and fish ponds surrounding the castle, favourably commented upon by contemporaries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg)

The state apartments (left), library (centre) and gatehouse (right)

William Herbert was executed as a Yorkist supporter in 1469 after the [Battle of Edgecote Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edgecote_Moor "Battle of Edgecote Moor"). Building work may have stopped for a period under his son, also called [William Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Pembroke "William Herbert, 2nd Earl of Pembroke"), before recommencing in the late 1470s.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-18) By 1492, the castle passed to [Elizabeth Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Somerset,_Baroness_Herbert "Elizabeth Somerset, Baroness Herbert"), William Herbert's daughter, who married Sir [Charles Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Somerset,_1st_Earl_of_Worcester "Charles Somerset, 1st Earl of Worcester"), passing the castle into a new family line.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19)

Sir Charles Somerset was politically successful under both [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") and [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England"), being made the [Earl of Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Worcester "Earl of Worcester").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) His son, [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_2nd_Earl_of_Worcester "Henry Somerset, 2nd Earl of Worcester"), died shortly after inheriting Raglan, but not before using [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead") reclaimed from [Tintern Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tintern_Abbey "Tintern Abbey") to help the building work at Raglan Castle during the [dissolution of the monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_monasteries "Dissolution of the monasteries").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) His son and grandson, [William Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Somerset,_3rd_Earl_of_Worcester "William Somerset, 3rd Earl of Worcester") and [Edward Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Somerset,_4th_Earl_of_Worcester "Edward Somerset, 4th Earl of Worcester"), proved to be what John Kenyon describes as "wealthy, brilliant and cultured men".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) William rebuilt much of the Pitched Stone Court, including the hall, adding the Long Gallery and developing the gardens into the new [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture") style.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-20) The Somerset family owned two key castles in the region, Raglan and [Chepstow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chepstow_Castle "Chepstow Castle"), and these appeared to have figured prominently as important status symbols in paintings owned by the family.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-21)

### 17th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 17th century")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png/250px-Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png)

Aerial photograph, showing the defences constructed during the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"); red and blue triangles represent the location of Parliamentarian and Royalist earthwork [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"); A and B indicate the locations of the Parliamentary and Royalist artillery batteries.

Edward Somerset made minor improvements to the interior of the castle at the start of the 17th century, but focused primarily on the exterior, expanding and developing the gardens and building the moat walk around the Great Tower.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.17-22) The resulting gardens were considered the equal of any others in the kingdom at the time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23)

Upon inheriting Raglan in 1628, [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_1st_Marquess_of_Worcester "Henry Somerset, 1st Marquess of Worcester"), then the 5th Earl of Worcester, continued to live a grand lifestyle in the castle in the 1630s, with a host of staff, including a steward, Master of Horse, Master of Fishponds, surveyors, auditors, ushers, a falconer and many footmen.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP1-24) The interior walls were hung with rich tapestries from [Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arras "Arras") in France, while an inventory taken in 1639 recorded a large number of silver and gilt plate kept in the Great Tower, including an ostrich egg cup,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-25) and a silver basket for oranges and lemons, then luxury items in Wales.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP3-26) Mead was a popular drink in the castle, but contemporaries described the castle as being a particular sober and respectful community.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-27) Henry developed the entrance route to the castle, including building the Red Gate.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23) His son [Edward, Lord Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Somerset,_2nd_Marquess_of_Worcester "Edward Somerset, 2nd Marquess of Worcester") became famous for building a "[water commanding machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_engine "Steam engine")" in the Great Tower, which used steam to pump a huge spout of water high into the air from the moat.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23)

In August 1642 the First English Civil War began between [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavaliers "Cavaliers") supporters of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") and [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England"). Raglan Castle was still held by Henry, then an elderly man, supported by his son, Lord Herbert.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP1-24) Both men were firm royalists.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP1-24) King Charles sent his own son, Prince [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), on a fund-raising tour of friendly regions, starting with Raglan Castle in October 1642, following which Henry was promoted to be the first [Marquess of Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquess_of_Worcester "Marquess of Worcester").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP3-26) Tensions grew in the immediate region, partially driven by religious tensions between some of the more [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") local people and the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") Marquess; on one of these occasions a local group attempted to search the castle, but were reportedly driven away by the sudden noise of Lord Herbert's steam-engine.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-28) The defences of Raglan were improved after this, with [modern earthwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_fort "Star fort")[bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") built around the castle and a [powder mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_mill "Powder mill") created; a garrison of around 300 men was established at a cost of £40,000.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-29)[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-31) Heavier cannon were installed in the bastions, with lighter pieces placed in the castle towers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.20-32)

Lord Herbert left the castle to join the campaign against Parliament, returning at intervals to acquire more funds for the war.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-33) Charles I himself visited the castle twice, first in June 1645 after the [battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby") and again in 1646, when he enjoyed playing [bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowls "Bowls") on the castle's green.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-34) The Royalist cause was now close to military collapse, and the Marquess started to send some valuables, including the oak panelling from the parlour, some plaster ceiling and many pictures, to his brother at nearby [Troy House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_House "Troy House") for safe-keeping.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP8-35) Lord Herbert was captured in Ireland, and an attack on Raglan itself appeared imminent.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP8-35)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/The_hexagonal_Great_Tower%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg/250px-The_hexagonal_Great_Tower%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_hexagonal_Great_Tower,_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg)

The [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting") side of the Great Tower

In expectation of a siege, the castle garrison was increased to around 800 soldiers; the avenue of trees outside the castle gates were cut down, and neighbouring buildings destroyed to prevent their being used by Parliamentary forces.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-36) Large amounts of food were brought in to support the growing castle community, which also included a number of the wider Herbert family and other regional Royalist leaders who had sought shelter there.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP9-37) The first Parliamentary army arrived in early June, under the command of Colonel Morgan and Sir [Trevor Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Trevor_Williams,_1st_Baronet "Sir Trevor Williams, 1st Baronet").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-38) After several calls for the castle to surrender, a siege ensued, lasting through the summer months.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP9-37) In August, additional Parliamentarian forces under General [Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax,_3rd_Lord_Fairfax_of_Cameron "Thomas Fairfax, 3rd Lord Fairfax of Cameron") arrived, and calls for the castle to surrender were renewed.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Fairfax's men began to dig trenches towards the castle, and used these to move [mortars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(weapon) "Mortar (weapon)") forward, probably including the famous "[Roaring Meg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roaring_Meg_(cannon) "Roaring Meg (cannon)")", bringing the interior of the castle into artillery range.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Facing a hopeless situation, the Marquess surrendered the castle on 19 August on relatively generous terms for the garrison.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP11-39) The Marquess himself was arrested and sent to [Windsor Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Castle "Windsor Castle"), where he died shortly afterwards.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Informed shortly before his death that Parliament had granted his request to be buried in the [family vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Chapel,_Windsor_Castle "St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle") at Windsor, the Marquess remarked; "Why then I shall have a better castle when I am dead, than they took from me when alive."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-ClarkP64-40)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Raglan_Castle_%280245%29.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_%280245%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_(0245).jpg)

The buttress in the Pitched Stone Court was damaged during the slighting of the castle. Archaeologist Lila Rakoczy suggested that the depth of the stone being removed indicates that a statue or decorative form of stone was originally present, and the removal of high-status and visually prominent material would have been a symbolic act.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-41)

Fairfax ordered the castle to be totally destroyed under the supervision of Henry Herbert, a descendant of William ap Thomas.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP12-42) The fortifications proved too strong, however, and only a few of the walls were destroyed, or [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-TribeP12-42) Historian Matthew Johnson describes the event as having the atmosphere of a "community festival", as local people dredged the castle moat in search of treasure, and emptied the fishponds of valuable [carp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carp "Carp").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-43) The [castle's library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Library "Raglan Library"), including an important collection of Welsh documents and books, was either stolen or destroyed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.20-32)

Despite some immediate confiscations after the siege, by the time of the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_(England) "Restoration (England)") of [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), the Somerset family had managed to recover most of their possessions, including Raglan Castle.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P22-44)[Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_1st_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 1st Duke of Beaufort"), the 3rd Marquess, decided to prioritise the rebuilding of his other houses at [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_House "Troy House") and [Badminton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton_House "Badminton House"), rather than Raglan, reusing some of the property sent away for safety before the war, or salvaged after the slighting.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P22-44)

### 18th to 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 18th to 21st centuries")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Raglan_Castle_%283375041%29.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_%283375041%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_(3375041).jpg)

Engraving of the state of the castle in 1798

For the first half of the 18th century, the castle continued to deteriorate, with the Somerset family allowing their stewards to quarry stone from the castle for the repair of other estate buildings.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-45) One particular estate surveyor called Hopkins became known as the "Grand Dilapidator", due to the number of chimneys, window frames and staircases he had removed from the castle.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46)[Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_5th_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 5th Duke of Beaufort"), the 5th Duke, finally put an end to this practice in 1756, and the castle became a tourist attraction, part of the popular [Wye Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Tour "Wye Tour").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46) Seats, fences and bridges were installed, and the first guidebook to the site was published in the early 19th century.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg/250px-Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg)

The Great Hall was temporarily re-roofed in the 1820s, when the castle was used for a "Grand Entertainment" by the Somersets, and in 1830 [Jeffrey Wyattville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Wyattville "Jeffrey Wyattville") was employed to reinstate the Grand Staircase.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-47) The Monmouthshire antiquarian [Joseph Bradney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bradney "Joseph Bradney") recorded a visit to the castle by [Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VII "Edward VII") and [Queen Alexandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_of_Denmark "Alexandra of Denmark"), then [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales") and [Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_of_Wales "Princess of Wales") of Wales, in October 1881.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Bradney1992P31-48) In 1938 [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_10th_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 10th Duke of Beaufort"), the 10th Duke, entrusted guardianship of Raglan Castle to the [Commissioner of Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Commissioner_of_Works "First Commissioner of Works"),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Newman2000P491-49) and the castle became a permanent tourist attraction.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46) Today, the castle is classed as a Grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") and as a [Scheduled Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduled_Monument "Scheduled Monument"), administered by [Cadw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw "Cadw").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-51) Between 2003 and 2007 Cambrian Archaeological Projects led excavations at the castle in advance of a planned new visitor centre.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-52) Since 2024, [Cadw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw "Cadw") are to standardise the name in both languages, to use the Welsh name _Castell Rhaglan_ in English.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Cadw_name-2) Although they have not yet done so as of 2026.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Cadw-3)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Raglan_diagram.png/250px-Raglan_diagram.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_diagram.png)

Plan of the castle, after [Augustus Pugin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Welby_Northmore_Pugin "Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin"): A – Great Tower; B – Moat; C – Gatehouse and bridge; D – Closet Tower; E – Pitched Stone Court; F – Office wing; G – Pantry; H – Kitchen; I – Parlour; J – Hall; K – Buttery; L – Long Gallery; M – Fountain Court; N – Apartments; O – South Gate and bridge; P – Moat walk

Raglan Castle was built in several phases, initial work occurring in the 1420s and 1430s, a major phase in the 1460s, with various alterations and additions at the end of the 16th century. The castle was built in stone, initially pale [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") from [Redbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redbrook "Redbrook"), and later [Old Red Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Red_Sandstone "Old Red Sandstone"), with [Bath Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_Stone "Bath Stone") used for many of the detailed features.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-53) Like similar properties of the period, the castle of the 1460s was almost certainly designed to be approached and entered in a particular way, maximising the aesthetic and political value of the fortification.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP85-54) At Raglan, the design highlighted the Great Tower: a typical senior visitor would ride through [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") village, and first the tower and then the rest of the castle would appear suddenly over the slight rise on the hill.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP85-54) A visitor would have needed to circle the Great Tower and the moat, before coming in through the gatehouse, into the Pitched Stone Court, around the edge of the communal hall, before reaching the previously hidden, and more refined, inner Fountain Court.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) Only then would a privileged guest be able to enter the Great Tower itself, overlooking the Herbert family's own chambers.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) Many less senior visitors or servants would never have entered this far, seeing only the external elements of the castle, but perhaps having been impressed by the outside of the Great Tower as they arrived.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55)

There has been much discussion amongst academics about the extent to which Raglan was influenced by contemporary French designs; one school of thought suggests that it was heavily influenced by designs that were then popular in the south of France; others oppose this "diffusionist" school of thought, and argue that there is insufficient evidence to draw such a conclusion.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Emery2006P291-56)[[nb 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-57) Another line of debate has been over the nature of the castle's defences, in particular its [gunloops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunloop "Gunloop").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-58) Many castles built around the same time as Raglan appear to have been built with less concern for defences than in the past, their military features more symbolic than real. At Raglan, there are numerous gunloops throughout the castle's defences, but many were ill-placed if the intention was to use them in a conflict; some could barely have been used at all.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-KingP168-59) Traditionally, an evolutionary explanation for this was given: Raglan's gunloops were of an early period, later surpassed in other castles.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-KingP168-59) More recent explanations emphasise the prestigious symbolism of gunloops for the Herbert family when they built the castle, even if many might have been impossible to use.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-60) Anthony Emery notes that Raglan's gunloops were better sited than many at the time, and at least "the owner was up to date in his symbolism"; Robert Liddiard suggests that the poor placing of some of the gunloops for aesthetic purposes might have actually been a conversation point for those visitors with experience of fighting in France and the "correct" placing of such defences.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-61)

### Gatehouse and Closet Tower

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Gatehouse and Closet Tower")]

The three-storey gatehouse to Raglan Castle dates from the 1460s and is approached over a stone bridge restored in 1949.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-62) Characterised by extensive [machicolations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation") and gunloops, the gatehouse would originally have had a twin-set of [portcullises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portcullis "Portcullis") and a [drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-63) The intention of the design was at least partially defensive, but was also intended to provide a dramatic and impressive entrance for senior visitors to the castle.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P27-64) The upper part of the gatehouse provided chambers for the constable of the castle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9) Immediately to the west of the gatehouse was the castle library, once famous for its collection of Welsh literature.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-65) On the east side of the gatehouse is the three-storey Closet Tower; this was designed to be integral to the gatehouse, and may have contained the original castle treasury, conveniently accessible by the constable.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P30-66) The Closet Tower was partly altered in later years, possibly to allow the basement to be used as a [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_(artillery) "Magazine (artillery)") in the English Civil War.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P30-66)

### Pitched Stone Court and Fountain Court

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Pitched Stone Court and Fountain Court")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg/330px-Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court,_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg)

The west side of the Pitched Stone Court, with the hall and its [oriel window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriel_window "Oriel window") at left

The Pitched Stone Court forms the north-east corner of the castle, and provided a centre for the castle services and servants; it takes its name from the late-Tudor [cobbling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobblestone "Cobblestone"), or pitched stones.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P32-67) On the east side of the court is the former office wing, a 16th-century construction mostly destroyed during the siege of 1646.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P32-67) The castle kitchens and pantries are on the north side, containing two large fireplaces and storage facilities for food and supplies in their cellars.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-68) In the 1460s, the first floors to these buildings included chambers for the senior servants.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-69) The buttery in the north-west corner would have been used to store and serve beer and wine.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-70)

On the south-west side of the court is the hall, a 16th-century design incorporating an earlier hall on the same site.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P38-71)64 by 28 feet (19.5 by 8.5 metres) wide, the hall was originally 42 feet (13 metres) high, with a roof made of Irish [oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak "Oak"), lit and ventilated by a [cupola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola "Cupola") in the middle.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Pugin,_p.26-72) A large [oriel window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriel_window "Oriel window") lit the end of the hall occupied at dinner by the earls of Worcester, which by the time Raglan was built would have been used only for larger formal occasions.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-73) Originally, the hall would have been fitted with carved wooden panelling and a [minstrel's gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minstrel's_gallery "Minstrel's gallery").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P38-71) The Fountain Court lies to the west of the Pitched Stone Court, and is named after a [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") fountain that once stood in the centre of it, featuring a white horse on a black marble base, complete with a flow of running water.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-74) The fountain was probably installed somewhat after the initial construction of the court in the 1460s, dating instead to Edward Somerset in the late 16th century; the horse symbolised Edward's prestigious role as [Master of the Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_the_Horse "Master of the Horse").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-75) The Fountain Court was built to provide luxurious accommodation for the family and guests—by the 15th century, it was important to be able to provide private chambers for visitors, and this court could hold up to four distinct groups of visitors in comfort.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-76) The Fountain Court as a whole is marked by what [Augustus Pugin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Pugin "Augustus Pugin") described as extremely fine, elegant and delicate stonework.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-77)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg)

The Grand Staircase to the west of Fountain Court, restored between 2010 and 2011

The castle [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel "Chapel") runs alongside the east side of the court, 41 feet (12 metres) long and originally laid with bright yellow and tiles and decorated with gold and silver vestments.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-78) The Long Gallery stretches across the whole east first-floor of the Fountain Court and, although now ruined, would have been a show-piece for the earls' wealth and power.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-79) The gallery was 126 feet (38 metres) long and during the Tudor period it would have been wood-panelled throughout and lined with tapestries and paintings.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-80) The Long Gallery was intended to allow family and guests to relax inside and to admire the gardens, water gardens and the deer park to the north of the castle.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) Although most of this decoration has since been lost, two [caryatid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryatid "Caryatid") statues can still be seen on the walls of the Long Gallery, modelled on a work by the French artist Hugues Sambin.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-82)

The west side of the Fountain Court comprises the apartments, with a number of bay windows and window seats facing west and north across the park.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-83) The Grand Staircase divides the apartments; restored between 2010 and 2011, the staircase would originally have had a substantial porch, similar to the one that survives in the Pitched Stone Court, and would have been a centre-piece of the Fountain Court.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-84) Although examples of such straight-flight staircases can be found in other late-medieval buildings, the architectural historian John Newman considers the Grand Staircase had "a grandeur hard to parallel in 15th-century England."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-85) The apartments to the west of the staircase are more complex than the others, designed to create somewhat greater privacy, and overlooked the gardens to the west of the castle.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-86) On the south side of the court is the South Gate, the original entrance to the castle prior to the 1460s reconstruction.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P46-87) The [fan-vaulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_vault "Fan vault") gatehouse closely resembles the contemporary cloisters at [Gloucester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester_Cathedral "Gloucester Cathedral"), but by the 16th century had been converted to the entrance to the bowling green in the terrace beyond.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P46-87)

On the south-east side of the court were the 16th-century parlour on the first-floor, and the dining room above it—both 49 by 21 feet (14.9 by 6.4 m).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-88) These were intended to provide rooms that were more private than the main hall, but more public than a personal chamber.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-89) Now ruined, they would originally have been decorated with carved [wainscoting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wainscot "Wainscot") and elaborate, carved chimney-pieces.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-90) Alongside these rooms, overlooking the Great Tower, were the private rooms for the lord's family, of higher quality than the other accommodation in the castle. Some of the carved badges and shields on the external walls of these state apartments still remain intact, as in the hall; these were a popular contemporary feature of 15th-century great castles, and would have created a similar effect to those at [Warkworth Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warkworth_Castle "Warkworth Castle") in Northumberland and [Raby Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raby_Castle "Raby Castle") in County Durham.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-91)

### Great Tower

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Great Tower")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG/250px-Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG)

View from the top of the Great Tower, showing the thick walls, the remains of the apron wall and a turret, the moat, the moat walk and a space for a classical statue

The Great Tower at Raglan Castle, sometimes called the Yellow Tower of Gwent, sits outside the rest of the castle, protected by a moat and linked to the Fountain Court by a bridge.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.49-92) The fortification is representative of a trend during the 15th and 16th centuries in British castle building: tower keeps such as this, large, solid buildings designed for private accommodation, probably inspired by those in France, had started to appear in the 14th century at [Dudley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudley_Castle "Dudley Castle") and Warkworth.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-93) In the 15th century the fashion spread, with the creation of French-influenced palatial castles featuring complex tower keeps, such as those at [Wardour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardour_Castle "Wardour Castle") and [Tattershall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tattershall_Castle "Tattershall Castle").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Pounds1994P271-94) These were expensive buildings to construct, each built to a unique design and, as historian Norman Pounds has suggested, "were designed to allow very rich men to live in luxury and splendour".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-95)

The hexagonal Great Tower was probably begun in the 1430s and 1440s, possibly on the motte of a previous castle.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-96) The tower today has lost not only one of its walls but part of its upper structure, and would originally have been three storeys high with probably additional machicolations on top similar to those on the gatehouse.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-97) It was designed to be a self-contained fortification, with its own water and food supplies, and luxurious quarters lit by large windows on the upper floors.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-98) Originally the tower was reached by a [bascule drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bascule_bridge "Bascule bridge"), usually considered to be drawn from contemporary French designs, such as those at [Ferté-Milon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Fert%C3%A9-Milon "La Ferté-Milon") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) This drawbridge was designed to have two parts—a wide, heavy bridge that would be raised or lowered when the family was in residence, and a thinner bridge, easier to lift, designed for the use of servants at other times.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) The Herberts used the bridge as their badge, and it can be seen in the carved window designs around the castle.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-99) The drawbridge was replaced with a grander stone bridge in the 1460s, probably at a cost of around £900 to £1000.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.49-92)[[nb 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-100) An apron wall with six turrets was also added around the tower at around the same time.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101)

The original moat around the tower would have been a simple design, but it was redesigned in the 1460s to provide a walkway around the outside of the Great Tower. The niches in the walls of the walkway are of 17th-century origin, and would originally have held [classical statues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_sculpture "Classical sculpture")—the walkway would have provided a dignified way of admiring the Great Tower.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101) It is likely that fish would have been bred in the moat.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101)

### Landscape and gardens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Landscape and gardens")]

The former 16th- and 17th-century gardens of Raglan Castle are still visible in the form of several long [terraces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_garden "Terrace garden") to the north of the castle, overlooking the lower ground beyond. First created in the second half of the 16th century, these terraces would originally have included a number of [knot gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_garden "Knot garden"), probably with [Italianate sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Italy "Culture of Italy") and carved stone balustrades.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) The gardens at their peak would have probably resembled those at [Nonsuch Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonsuch_Palace "Nonsuch Palace"), where the Somersets also had an interest as the royal keepers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.17-22) The valley below retains some signs of the drainage ditches that once formed part of the [water gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_garden "Water garden") that flooded the bottom of the site, although the original "water-parterre" to the north-west of the castle, another water garden in the south, and the extensive gardens around the south-west of the castle are now no longer visible.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) The castle's [bowling green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_green "Bowling green") still survives, on a terrace just beyond the South Gate entrance.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-102) The castle's parks reverted to agricultural use by the 19th century, and Raglan is now surrounded by fields.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-Pugin,_p.26-72) The gardens and park at Raglan are designated Grade I on the [Cadw/ICOMOS Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw/ICOMOS_Register_of_Parks_and_Gardens_of_Special_Historic_Interest_in_Wales "Cadw/ICOMOS Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in Wales").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Castle#cite_note-103)
