**Raglan Castle** ([Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language"): _Castell Rhaglan_)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Cadw_name-1) is a [late medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages")[castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle") located just north of the village of [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") in the county of [Monmouthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouthshire "Monmouthshire") in south east [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"). The modern castle dates from between the 15th and early 17th centuries, when the successive ruling families of the [Herberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Herbert "Baron Herbert") and the [Somersets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Beaufort "Duke of Beaufort") created a luxurious, fortified castle, complete with a large hexagonal [keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep"), known as the Great Tower or the Yellow Tower of [Gwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Gwent "Kingdom of Gwent"). Surrounded by [parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park"), [water gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_garden "Water garden") and [terraces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_garden "Terrace garden"), the castle was considered by contemporaries to be the equal of any other in England or Wales.

During the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"), Raglan was occupied by a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") garrison on behalf of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") but was taken by [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") forces in 1646 and its walls [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting"), or deliberately put beyond military use. After the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in 1660, the Somersets declined to restore it and it became first a source of local building materials, then a [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") ruin. It is now a [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history of the castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history of the castle")]

Following the [Norman invasion of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_invasion_of_Wales "Norman invasion of Wales"), the area around the village of [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") was granted to [William FitzOsbern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_FitzOsbern,_1st_Earl_of_Hereford "William FitzOsbern, 1st Earl of Hereford"), the [Earl of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Hereford "Earl of Hereford").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P3-4) Some historians, such as John Kenyon, suspect that an early [motte and bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motte_and_bailey "Motte and bailey") castle may have been built on the Raglan site during this period: the location had strategic importance and archaeologists have discovered the remains of a possible bailey ditch on the site.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P3-4) The local manor was held by the Bloet family from the late 12th century until the late 14th century, and the family built a manor house somewhere on the site during this period, surrounded by a park.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-5) By the late medieval period the Raglan site was surrounded by the large [deer parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park") of Home Park and Red Deer Park, the latter being enclosed at the end of the period.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6)

### 15th to 16th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 15th to 16th centuries")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg/250px-Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Reconstruction.jpg)

Reconstruction of Raglan Castle around 1620

The current Raglan Castle was begun by [Sir William ap Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_ap_Thomas "William ap Thomas"), the lesser son of a minor Welsh family who rose through the ranks of mid-15th century politics, profiting from the benefits of the local offices he held.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-7) William married first Elizabeth, a wealthy heiress, and then Gwladus, another heiress who would prove to be a powerful regional figure in her own right.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-8) In 1432, [Sir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir "Sir") William purchased the manor of Raglan, where he had already been staying as a tenant, for 1,000 [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_(money) "Mark (money)") (£666 13s 4d) and commenced a programme of building work that established the basic shape of the castle as seen today, although most of it—with the exception of the South Gate and the Great Tower—was later built over.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-11)

Sir William's son dropped the Welsh version of his name, calling himself [William Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herbert,_1st_Earl_of_Pembroke_(1423%E2%80%931469) "William Herbert, 1st Earl of Pembroke (1423–1469)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9) He continued to rise in prominence, supporting the [House of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York") during the [War of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Roses "War of the Roses"), fighting in the [Hundred Years War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years_War "Hundred Years War") in France but making his fortune from the [Gascon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") wine trade.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-12) He was also closely associated with Welsh politics and status; he was the first Welshman to be made an earl and was described by contemporary poets as the "national deliverer" who might achieve Welsh independence.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-13) In the 1460s William used his increasing wealth to remodel Raglan on a much grander scale.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-14) The symbolism of the castle architecture may have reflected the Welsh family roots: historian Matthew Johnson has suggested that the polygonal towers were possibly designed to imitate those of [Caernarfon Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caernarfon_Castle "Caernarfon Castle"), whose architecture carries numerous allusions to the eventual return of a Roman Emperor to Wales.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-15) Historian Anthony Emery has described the resulting castle as one of the "last formidable displays of medieval defensive architecture".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-16)

There was an important link between Raglan Castle and the surrounding [parkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_deer_park "Medieval deer park"), in particular the Home Park and the Red Deer Park.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6) Historian Robert Liddiard suggests that on the basis of the views from the castle at this time, the structured nature of the parks would have contrasted with the wilderness of the mountain peaks framing the scene beyond, making an important statement about the refinement and cultured nature of the castle lord.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-17) In the 15th century there were also extensive orchards and fish ponds surrounding the castle, favourably commented upon by contemporaries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P11-6)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_Gatehouse_and_library.jpg)

The state apartments (left), library (centre) and gatehouse (right)

William Herbert was executed as a Yorkist supporter in 1469 after the [Battle of Edgecote Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Edgecote_Moor "Battle of Edgecote Moor"). Building work may have stopped for a period under his son, also called [William Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Pembroke "William Herbert, 2nd Earl of Pembroke"), before recommencing in the late 1470s.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-18) By 1492, the castle passed to [Elizabeth Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Somerset,_Baroness_Herbert "Elizabeth Somerset, Baroness Herbert"), William Herbert's daughter, who married Sir [Charles Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Somerset,_1st_Earl_of_Worcester "Charles Somerset, 1st Earl of Worcester"), passing the castle into a new family line.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19)

Sir Charles Somerset was politically successful under both [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") and [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England"), being made the [Earl of Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Worcester "Earl of Worcester").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) His son, [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_2nd_Earl_of_Worcester "Henry Somerset, 2nd Earl of Worcester"), died shortly after inheriting Raglan, but not before using [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead") reclaimed from [Tintern Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tintern_Abbey "Tintern Abbey") to help the building work at Raglan Castle during the [dissolution of the monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_monasteries "Dissolution of the monasteries").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) His son and grandson, [William Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Somerset,_3rd_Earl_of_Worcester "William Somerset, 3rd Earl of Worcester") and [Edward Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Somerset,_4th_Earl_of_Worcester "Edward Somerset, 4th Earl of Worcester"), proved to be what John Kenyon describes as "wealthy, brilliant and cultured men".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P13-19) William rebuilt much of the Pitched Stone Court, including the hall, adding the Long Gallery and developing the gardens into the new [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture") style.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-20) The Somerset family owned two key castles in the region, Raglan and [Chepstow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chepstow_Castle "Chepstow Castle"), and these appeared to have figured prominently as important status symbols in paintings owned by the family.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-21)

### 17th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 17th century")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png/250px-Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_Civil_War_bastons.png)

Aerial photograph, showing the defences constructed during the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"); red and blue triangles represent the location of Parliamentarian and Royalist earthwork [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion"); A and B indicate the locations of the Parliamentary and Royalist artillery batteries.

Edward Somerset made minor improvements to the interior of the castle at the start of the 17th century, but focused primarily on the exterior, expanding and developing the gardens and building the moat walk around the Great Tower.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.17-22) The resulting gardens were considered the equal of any others in the kingdom at the time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23)

Upon inheriting Raglan in 1628, [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_1st_Marquess_of_Worcester "Henry Somerset, 1st Marquess of Worcester"), then the 5th Earl of Worcester, continued to live a grand lifestyle in the castle in the 1630s, with a host of staff, including a steward, Master of Horse, Master of Fishponds, surveyors, auditors, ushers, a falconer and many footmen.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP1-24) The interior walls were hung with rich tapestries from [Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arras "Arras") in France, while an inventory taken in 1639 recorded a large number of silver and gilt plate kept in the Great Tower, including an ostrich egg cup,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-25) and a silver basket for oranges and lemons, then luxury items in Wales.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP3-26) Mead was a popular drink in the castle, but contemporaries described the castle as being a particular sober and respectful community.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-27) Henry developed the entrance route to the castle, including building the Red Gate.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23) His son [Edward, Lord Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Somerset,_2nd_Marquess_of_Worcester "Edward Somerset, 2nd Marquess of Worcester") became famous for building a "[water commanding machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_engine "Steam engine")" in the Great Tower, which used steam to pump a huge spout of water high into the air from the moat.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P18-23)

In August 1642 the First English Civil War began between [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavaliers "Cavaliers") supporters of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") and [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England"). Raglan Castle was still held by Henry, then an elderly man, supported by his son, Lord Herbert.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP1-24) Both men were firm royalists.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP1-24) King Charles sent his own son, Prince [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), on a fund-raising tour of friendly regions, starting with Raglan Castle in October 1642, following which Henry was promoted to be the first [Marquess of Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquess_of_Worcester "Marquess of Worcester").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP3-26) Tensions grew in the immediate region, partially driven by religious tensions between some of the more [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") local people and the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") Marquess; on one of these occasions a local group attempted to search the castle, but were reportedly driven away by the sudden noise of Lord Herbert's steam-engine.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-28) The defences of Raglan were improved after this, with [modern earthwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_fort "Star fort")[bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") built around the castle and a [powder mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_mill "Powder mill") created; a garrison of around 300 men was established at a cost of £40,000.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-29)[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-31) Heavier cannon were installed in the bastions, with lighter pieces placed in the castle towers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.20-32)

Lord Herbert left the castle to join the campaign against Parliament, returning at intervals to acquire more funds for the war.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-33) Charles I himself visited the castle twice, first in June 1645 after the [battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby") and again in 1646, when he enjoyed playing [bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowls "Bowls") on the castle's green.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-34) The Royalist cause was now close to military collapse, and the Marquess started to send some valuables, including the oak panelling from the parlour, some plaster ceiling and many pictures, to his brother at nearby [Troy House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_House "Troy House") for safe-keeping.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP8-35) Lord Herbert was captured in Ireland, and an attack on Raglan itself appeared imminent.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP8-35)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/The_hexagonal_Great_Tower%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg/250px-The_hexagonal_Great_Tower%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_hexagonal_Great_Tower,_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531739.jpg)

The [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting") side of the Great Tower

In expectation of a siege, the castle garrison was increased to around 800 soldiers; the avenue of trees outside the castle gates were cut down, and neighbouring buildings destroyed to prevent their being used by Parliamentary forces.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-36) Large amounts of food were brought in to support the growing castle community, which also included a number of the wider Herbert family and other regional Royalist leaders who had sought shelter there.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP9-37) The first Parliamentary army arrived in early June, under the command of Colonel Morgan and Sir [Trevor Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Trevor_Williams,_1st_Baronet "Sir Trevor Williams, 1st Baronet").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-38) After several calls for the castle to surrender, a siege ensued, lasting through the summer months.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP9-37) In August, additional Parliamentarian forces under General [Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax,_3rd_Lord_Fairfax_of_Cameron "Thomas Fairfax, 3rd Lord Fairfax of Cameron") arrived, and calls for the castle to surrender were renewed.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Fairfax's men began to dig trenches towards the castle, and used these to move [mortars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(weapon) "Mortar (weapon)") forward, probably including the famous "[Roaring Meg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roaring_Meg_(cannon) "Roaring Meg (cannon)")", bringing the interior of the castle into artillery range.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Facing a hopeless situation, the Marquess surrendered the castle on 19 August on relatively generous terms for the garrison.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP11-39) The Marquess himself was arrested and sent to [Windsor Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Castle "Windsor Castle"), where he died shortly afterwards.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP11-39) Informed shortly before his death that Parliament had granted his request to be buried in the [family vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Chapel,_Windsor_Castle "St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle") at Windsor, the Marquess remarked; "Why then I shall have a better castle when I am dead, than they took from me when alive."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-ClarkP64-40)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Raglan_Castle_%280245%29.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_%280245%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_(0245).jpg)

The buttress in the Pitched Stone Court was damaged during the slighting of the castle. Archaeologist Lila Rakoczy suggested that the depth of the stone being removed indicates that a statue or decorative form of stone was originally present, and the removal of high-status and visually prominent material would have been a symbolic act.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-41)

Fairfax ordered the castle to be totally destroyed under the supervision of Henry Herbert, a descendant of William ap Thomas.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP12-42) The fortifications proved too strong, however, and only a few of the walls were destroyed, or [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-TribeP12-42) Historian Matthew Johnson describes the event as having the atmosphere of a "community festival", as local people dredged the castle moat in search of treasure, and emptied the fishponds of valuable [carp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carp "Carp").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-43) The [castle's library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan_Library "Raglan Library"), including an important collection of Welsh documents and books, was either stolen or destroyed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.20-32)

Despite some immediate confiscations after the siege, by the time of the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_(England) "Restoration (England)") of [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), the Somerset family had managed to recover most of their possessions, including Raglan Castle.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P22-44)[Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_1st_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 1st Duke of Beaufort"), the 3rd Marquess, decided to prioritise the rebuilding of his other houses at [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_House "Troy House") and [Badminton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton_House "Badminton House"), rather than Raglan, reusing some of the property sent away for safety before the war, or salvaged after the slighting.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P22-44)

### 18th to 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 18th to 21st centuries")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Raglan_Castle_%283375041%29.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_%283375041%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_(3375041).jpg)

Engraving of the state of the castle in 1798

For the first half of the 18th century, the castle continued to deteriorate, with the Somerset family allowing their stewards to quarry stone from the castle for the repair of other estate buildings.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-45) One particular estate surveyor called Hopkins became known as the "Grand Dilapidator", due to the number of chimneys, window frames and staircases he had removed from the castle.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46)[Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_5th_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 5th Duke of Beaufort"), the 5th Duke, finally put an end to this practice in 1756, and the castle became a tourist attraction, part of the popular [Wye Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Tour "Wye Tour").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46) Seats, fences and bridges were installed, and the first guidebook to the site was published in the early 19th century.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg/250px-Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ragland_castle_on_porcelain.jpg)

The Great Hall was temporarily re-roofed in the 1820s, when the castle was used for a "Grand Entertainment" by the Somersets, and in 1830 [Jeffrey Wyattville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Wyattville "Jeffrey Wyattville") was employed to reinstate the Grand Staircase.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-47) The Monmouthshire antiquarian [Joseph Bradney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bradney "Joseph Bradney") recorded a visit to the castle by [Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VII "Edward VII") and [Queen Alexandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_of_Denmark "Alexandra of Denmark"), then [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales") and [Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_of_Wales "Princess of Wales") of Wales, in October 1881.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Bradney1992P31-48) In 1938 [Henry Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_10th_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 10th Duke of Beaufort"), the 10th Duke, entrusted guardianship of Raglan Castle to the [Commissioner of Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Commissioner_of_Works "First Commissioner of Works"),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Newman2000P491-49) and the castle became a permanent tourist attraction.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P23-46) Today, the castle is classed as a Grade I [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") and as a [Scheduled Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduled_Monument "Scheduled Monument"), administered by [Cadw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw "Cadw").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-51) Between 2003 and 2007 Cambrian Archaeological Projects led excavations at the castle in advance of a planned new visitor centre.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-52) Since 2024, [Cadw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw "Cadw") are to standardise the name in both languages, to use the Welsh name _Castell Rhaglan_ in English.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Cadw_name-2) Although they have not yet done so as of 2026.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Cadw-3)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Raglan_diagram.png/250px-Raglan_diagram.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_diagram.png)

Plan of the castle, after [Augustus Pugin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Welby_Northmore_Pugin "Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin"): A – Great Tower; B – Moat; C – Gatehouse and bridge; D – Closet Tower; E – Pitched Stone Court; F – Office wing; G – Pantry; H – Kitchen; I – Parlour; J – Hall; K – Buttery; L – Long Gallery; M – Fountain Court; N – Apartments; O – South Gate and bridge; P – Moat walk

Raglan Castle was built in several phases, initial work occurring in the 1420s and 1430s, a major phase in the 1460s, with various alterations and additions at the end of the 16th century. The castle was built in stone, initially pale [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone") from [Redbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redbrook "Redbrook"), and later [Old Red Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Red_Sandstone "Old Red Sandstone"), with [Bath Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_Stone "Bath Stone") used for many of the detailed features.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-53) Like similar properties of the period, the castle of the 1460s was almost certainly designed to be approached and entered in a particular way, maximising the aesthetic and political value of the fortification.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP85-54) At Raglan, the design highlighted the Great Tower: a typical senior visitor would ride through [Raglan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raglan,_Monmouthshire "Raglan, Monmouthshire") village, and first the tower and then the rest of the castle would appear suddenly over the slight rise on the hill.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP85-54) A visitor would have needed to circle the Great Tower and the moat, before coming in through the gatehouse, into the Pitched Stone Court, around the edge of the communal hall, before reaching the previously hidden, and more refined, inner Fountain Court.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) Only then would a privileged guest be able to enter the Great Tower itself, overlooking the Herbert family's own chambers.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) Many less senior visitors or servants would never have entered this far, seeing only the external elements of the castle, but perhaps having been impressed by the outside of the Great Tower as they arrived.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55)

There has been much discussion amongst academics about the extent to which Raglan was influenced by contemporary French designs; one school of thought suggests that it was heavily influenced by designs that were then popular in the south of France; others oppose this "diffusionist" school of thought, and argue that there is insufficient evidence to draw such a conclusion.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Emery2006P291-56)[[nb 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-57) Another line of debate has been over the nature of the castle's defences, in particular its [gunloops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunloop "Gunloop").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-58) Many castles built around the same time as Raglan appear to have been built with less concern for defences than in the past, their military features more symbolic than real. At Raglan, there are numerous gunloops throughout the castle's defences, but many were ill-placed if the intention was to use them in a conflict; some could barely have been used at all.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-KingP168-59) Traditionally, an evolutionary explanation for this was given: Raglan's gunloops were of an early period, later surpassed in other castles.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-KingP168-59) More recent explanations emphasise the prestigious symbolism of gunloops for the Herbert family when they built the castle, even if many might have been impossible to use.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-60) Anthony Emery notes that Raglan's gunloops were better sited than many at the time, and at least "the owner was up to date in his symbolism"; Robert Liddiard suggests that the poor placing of some of the gunloops for aesthetic purposes might have actually been a conversation point for those visitors with experience of fighting in France and the "correct" placing of such defences.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-61)

### Gatehouse and Closet Tower

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Gatehouse and Closet Tower")]

The three-storey gatehouse to Raglan Castle dates from the 1460s and is approached over a stone bridge restored in 1949.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-62) Characterised by extensive [machicolations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation") and gunloops, the gatehouse would originally have had a twin-set of [portcullises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portcullis "Portcullis") and a [drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-63) The intention of the design was at least partially defensive, but was also intended to provide a dramatic and impressive entrance for senior visitors to the castle.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P27-64) The upper part of the gatehouse provided chambers for the constable of the castle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P7-9) Immediately to the west of the gatehouse was the castle library, once famous for its collection of Welsh literature.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-65) On the east side of the gatehouse is the three-storey Closet Tower; this was designed to be integral to the gatehouse, and may have contained the original castle treasury, conveniently accessible by the constable.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P30-66) The Closet Tower was partly altered in later years, possibly to allow the basement to be used as a [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_(artillery) "Magazine (artillery)") in the English Civil War.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P30-66)

### Pitched Stone Court and Fountain Court

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Pitched Stone Court and Fountain Court")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg/330px-Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court%2C_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Partly-restored_windows_facing_the_Pitched_Stone_Court,_Raglan_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1531734.jpg)

The west side of the Pitched Stone Court, with the hall and its [oriel window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriel_window "Oriel window") at left

The Pitched Stone Court forms the north-east corner of the castle, and provided a centre for the castle services and servants; it takes its name from the late-Tudor [cobbling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobblestone "Cobblestone"), or pitched stones.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P32-67) On the east side of the court is the former office wing, a 16th-century construction mostly destroyed during the siege of 1646.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P32-67) The castle kitchens and pantries are on the north side, containing two large fireplaces and storage facilities for food and supplies in their cellars.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-68) In the 1460s, the first floors to these buildings included chambers for the senior servants.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-69) The buttery in the north-west corner would have been used to store and serve beer and wine.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-70)

On the south-west side of the court is the hall, a 16th-century design incorporating an earlier hall on the same site.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P38-71)64 by 28 feet (19.5 by 8.5 metres) wide, the hall was originally 42 feet (13 metres) high, with a roof made of Irish [oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak "Oak"), lit and ventilated by a [cupola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola "Cupola") in the middle.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Pugin,_p.26-72) A large [oriel window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriel_window "Oriel window") lit the end of the hall occupied at dinner by the earls of Worcester, which by the time Raglan was built would have been used only for larger formal occasions.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-73) Originally, the hall would have been fitted with carved wooden panelling and a [minstrel's gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minstrel's_gallery "Minstrel's gallery").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P38-71) The Fountain Court lies to the west of the Pitched Stone Court, and is named after a [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") fountain that once stood in the centre of it, featuring a white horse on a black marble base, complete with a flow of running water.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-74) The fountain was probably installed somewhat after the initial construction of the court in the 1460s, dating instead to Edward Somerset in the late 16th century; the horse symbolised Edward's prestigious role as [Master of the Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_the_Horse "Master of the Horse").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-75) The Fountain Court was built to provide luxurious accommodation for the family and guests—by the 15th century, it was important to be able to provide private chambers for visitors, and this court could hold up to four distinct groups of visitors in comfort.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-76) The Fountain Court as a whole is marked by what [Augustus Pugin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Pugin "Augustus Pugin") described as extremely fine, elegant and delicate stonework.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-77)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg/250px-Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_-_Grand_Staircase_-_1.jpg)

The Grand Staircase to the west of Fountain Court, restored between 2010 and 2011

The castle [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel "Chapel") runs alongside the east side of the court, 41 feet (12 metres) long and originally laid with bright yellow and tiles and decorated with gold and silver vestments.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-78) The Long Gallery stretches across the whole east first-floor of the Fountain Court and, although now ruined, would have been a show-piece for the earls' wealth and power.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-79) The gallery was 126 feet (38 metres) long and during the Tudor period it would have been wood-panelled throughout and lined with tapestries and paintings.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-80) The Long Gallery was intended to allow family and guests to relax inside and to admire the gardens, water gardens and the deer park to the north of the castle.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) Although most of this decoration has since been lost, two [caryatid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryatid "Caryatid") statues can still be seen on the walls of the Long Gallery, modelled on a work by the French artist Hugues Sambin.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-82)

The west side of the Fountain Court comprises the apartments, with a number of bay windows and window seats facing west and north across the park.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-83) The Grand Staircase divides the apartments; restored between 2010 and 2011, the staircase would originally have had a substantial porch, similar to the one that survives in the Pitched Stone Court, and would have been a centre-piece of the Fountain Court.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-84) Although examples of such straight-flight staircases can be found in other late-medieval buildings, the architectural historian John Newman considers the Grand Staircase had "a grandeur hard to parallel in 15th-century England."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-85) The apartments to the west of the staircase are more complex than the others, designed to create somewhat greater privacy, and overlooked the gardens to the west of the castle.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-86) On the south side of the court is the South Gate, the original entrance to the castle prior to the 1460s reconstruction.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P46-87) The [fan-vaulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_vault "Fan vault") gatehouse closely resembles the contemporary cloisters at [Gloucester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester_Cathedral "Gloucester Cathedral"), but by the 16th century had been converted to the entrance to the bowling green in the terrace beyond.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P46-87)

On the south-east side of the court were the 16th-century parlour on the first-floor, and the dining room above it—both 49 by 21 feet (14.9 by 6.4 m).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-88) These were intended to provide rooms that were more private than the main hall, but more public than a personal chamber.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-89) Now ruined, they would originally have been decorated with carved [wainscoting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wainscot "Wainscot") and elaborate, carved chimney-pieces.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-90) Alongside these rooms, overlooking the Great Tower, were the private rooms for the lord's family, of higher quality than the other accommodation in the castle. Some of the carved badges and shields on the external walls of these state apartments still remain intact, as in the hall; these were a popular contemporary feature of 15th-century great castles, and would have created a similar effect to those at [Warkworth Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warkworth_Castle "Warkworth Castle") in Northumberland and [Raby Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raby_Castle "Raby Castle") in County Durham.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-91)

### Great Tower

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Great Tower")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG/250px-Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raglan_Castle_tower_and_moat.JPG)

View from the top of the Great Tower, showing the thick walls, the remains of the apron wall and a turret, the moat, the moat walk and a space for a classical statue

The Great Tower at Raglan Castle, sometimes called the Yellow Tower of Gwent, sits outside the rest of the castle, protected by a moat and linked to the Fountain Court by a bridge.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.49-92) The fortification is representative of a trend during the 15th and 16th centuries in British castle building: tower keeps such as this, large, solid buildings designed for private accommodation, probably inspired by those in France, had started to appear in the 14th century at [Dudley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudley_Castle "Dudley Castle") and Warkworth.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-93) In the 15th century the fashion spread, with the creation of French-influenced palatial castles featuring complex tower keeps, such as those at [Wardour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardour_Castle "Wardour Castle") and [Tattershall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tattershall_Castle "Tattershall Castle").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Pounds1994P271-94) These were expensive buildings to construct, each built to a unique design and, as historian Norman Pounds has suggested, "were designed to allow very rich men to live in luxury and splendour".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-95)

The hexagonal Great Tower was probably begun in the 1430s and 1440s, possibly on the motte of a previous castle.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-96) The tower today has lost not only one of its walls but part of its upper structure, and would originally have been three storeys high with probably additional machicolations on top similar to those on the gatehouse.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-97) It was designed to be a self-contained fortification, with its own water and food supplies, and luxurious quarters lit by large windows on the upper floors.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-98) Originally the tower was reached by a [bascule drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bascule_bridge "Bascule bridge"), usually considered to be drawn from contemporary French designs, such as those at [Ferté-Milon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Fert%C3%A9-Milon "La Ferté-Milon") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) This drawbridge was designed to have two parts—a wide, heavy bridge that would be raised or lowered when the family was in residence, and a thinner bridge, easier to lift, designed for the use of servants at other times.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-JohnsonP86-55) The Herberts used the bridge as their badge, and it can be seen in the carved window designs around the castle.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-99) The drawbridge was replaced with a grander stone bridge in the 1460s, probably at a cost of around £900 to £1000.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.49-92)[[nb 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-100) An apron wall with six turrets was also added around the tower at around the same time.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101)

The original moat around the tower would have been a simple design, but it was redesigned in the 1460s to provide a walkway around the outside of the Great Tower. The niches in the walls of the walkway are of 17th-century origin, and would originally have held [classical statues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_sculpture "Classical sculpture")—the walkway would have provided a dignified way of admiring the Great Tower.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101) It is likely that fish would have been bred in the moat.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon2003P53-101)

### Landscape and gardens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Landscape and gardens")]

The former 16th- and 17th-century gardens of Raglan Castle are still visible in the form of several long [terraces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_garden "Terrace garden") to the north of the castle, overlooking the lower ground beyond. First created in the second half of the 16th century, these terraces would originally have included a number of [knot gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_garden "Knot garden"), probably with [Italianate sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Italy "Culture of Italy") and carved stone balustrades.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) The gardens at their peak would have probably resembled those at [Nonsuch Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonsuch_Palace "Nonsuch Palace"), where the Somersets also had an interest as the royal keepers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Kenyon_2003,_p.17-22) The valley below retains some signs of the drainage ditches that once formed part of the [water gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_garden "Water garden") that flooded the bottom of the site, although the original "water-parterre" to the north-west of the castle, another water garden in the south, and the extensive gardens around the south-west of the castle are now no longer visible.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Taylor_p.60-81) The castle's [bowling green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_green "Bowling green") still survives, on a terrace just beyond the South Gate entrance.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-102) The castle's parks reverted to agricultural use by the 19th century, and Raglan is now surrounded by fields.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-Pugin,_p.26-72) The gardens and park at Raglan are designated Grade I on the [Cadw/ICOMOS Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadw/ICOMOS_Register_of_Parks_and_Gardens_of_Special_Historic_Interest_in_Wales "Cadw/ICOMOS Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in Wales").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raglan_Castle&search=film#cite_note-103)

**Herstmonceux Castle** is a brick-built [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle"), dating from the 15th century, near [Herstmonceux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux "Herstmonceux"), [East Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Sussex "East Sussex"), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). It is one of the oldest significant brick buildings still standing in England.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) The castle was renowned for being one of the first buildings to use that material in England, built using bricks made from local clay by builders from Flanders.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-2) It dates from 1441.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3) Construction began under the then-owner, [Sir Roger Fiennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fiennes "Roger Fiennes"), and was continued after his death in 1449 by his son, [Lord Dacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Fiennes,_7th_Baron_Dacre "Richard Fiennes, 7th Baron Dacre").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3)

The castle was sold in 1708 to [George Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Naylor "George Naylor"). His descendant, Robert Hare-Naylor, had the interior of the castle demolished in 1776–77 to turn it into a picturesque landscape feature in the grounds of [Herstmonceux Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Place "Herstmonceux Place"). In the early twentieth century, the castle was restored in two separate building campaigns for Colonel [Claude Lowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lowther "Claude Lowther") and [Sir Paul Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Paul_Latham,_2nd_Baronet "Sir Paul Latham, 2nd Baronet"). Herstmonceux was gifted to [Queen's University at Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_at_Kingston "Queen's University at Kingston"), a Canadian university, in 1993 by Alfred and Isabel Bader.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-5)

The parks and gardens of Herstmonceux Castle and Place are Grade II* listed on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3) Other listed structures on the Herstmonceux estate include the Grade II listed walled garden to the north of the castle,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLEWallGarden-6) and the Grade II* listed telescopes and workshops of the Herstmonceux Science Centre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLEScience-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

The first written evidence of the existence of the Herst settlement appears in [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror")'s [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book") of 1086, which reports that one of William's closest supporters granted tenancy of the manor at Herst to a man named 'Wilbert'.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) By the end of the twelfth century, the family at the manor house at Herst had considerable status. Written accounts mention a lady called Idonea de Herst, who married a Norman nobleman named Ingelram de Monceux. Around this time, the manor began to be called the "Herst of the Monceux", a name that eventually became Herstmonceux.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1)

A descendant of the Monceux family, [Roger Fiennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fiennes "Roger Fiennes"), was ultimately responsible for the construction of Herstmonceux Castle in the County of Sussex. Sir Roger was appointed Treasurer of the Household of [Henry VI of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VI_of_England "Henry VI of England") and needed a house fitting a man of his position, so construction of the castle on the site of the old manor house began in 1441. It was this position as treasurer which enabled him to afford the £3,800 construction of the original castle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-8)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg/250px-Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg)

Floor plan of the original house; (l) ground floor, (r) first floor

In 1541, Sir Thomas Fiennes, Lord Dacre, was tried for murder and robbery of the King's deer after his poaching exploits on a neighboring estate resulted in the death of a gamekeeper. He was convicted and hanged as a [commoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commoner "Commoner"), and the Herstmonceux estate was temporarily confiscated by [Henry VIII of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England"), but was restored to the Fiennes family during the reign of one of Henry's children.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-9)

The profligacy of the 15th [Baron Dacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Dacre "Baron Dacre"), heir to the Fiennes family, forced him to sell in 1708 to [George Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Naylor "George Naylor"), a lawyer of [Lincoln's Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln's_Inn "Lincoln's Inn") in London. Bethaia Naylor, who became the heiress of Herstmonceux on the death of her brother's only daughter, married [Francis Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Hare_(bishop) "Francis Hare (bishop)") and produced a son, Francis, who inherited in turn, his mother's property. The castle eventually came into the possession of [Robert Hare-Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Hare-Naylor "Francis Hare-Naylor"), who, upon the insistence of his second wife, Henrietta Henckell, followed the architect [Samuel Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wyatt "Samuel Wyatt")'s advice to reduce the Castle to a picturesque ruin by demolishing the interior.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-10) Thomas Lennard, 17th Baron Dacre, was sufficiently exercised as to commission [James Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lambert_(painter) "James Lambert (painter)") of Lewes to record the building in 1776.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-12) The castle was dismantled in 1777 leaving the exterior walls standing and remained a ruin until the early 20th century.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-13)

### 20th-century restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 20th-century restoration")]

Radical restoration work was undertaken by Colonel [Claude Lowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lowther "Claude Lowther") in 1913 to transform the ruined building into a residence and, based on a design by the architect, [Walter Godfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Godfrey_(architect) "Walter Godfrey (architect)"), this work was completed by [Sir Paul Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Paul_Latham,_2nd_Baronet "Sir Paul Latham, 2nd Baronet") in 1933. The existing interiors largely date from that period, incorporating architectural antiques from England and France. The one major change in planning was the combination of the four internal [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") into one large one. The restoration work, regarded as the apex of Godfrey's architectural achievement, was described by the critic [Sir Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner") as executed 'exemplarily'.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-14)

### Royal Greenwich Observatory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Royal Greenwich Observatory")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg/250px-Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg)

Aerial view of the former Royal Greenwich Observatory at Herstmonceux; the six domes of the "Equatorial Group" of telescopes can be seen to the left, the former location of the [Isaac Newton Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton_Telescope "Isaac Newton Telescope") is the single dome to the right

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Royal_Greenwich_Observatory%2C_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg/250px-Royal_Greenwich_Observatory%2C_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Royal_Greenwich_Observatory,_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg)

The former Royal Greenwich Observatory at Herstmonceux

The [Royal Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Observatory,_Greenwich "Royal Observatory, Greenwich") was founded by King Charles II at [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich") in 1675.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-15) Observing conditions at Greenwich deteriorated following the urban growth of London, and plans were made in the early 20th century to relocate the observatory to a rural location with clearer, darker skies. Herstmonceux Castle and estate were put up for sale by their private owners and were sold in 1946 to the [Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Admiralty "British Admiralty"), which then operated the Royal Observatory on behalf of the British government. The relocation of the observatory took place over a decade, and was complete by 1957. A number of new buildings were erected in the castle grounds, most notably the domes of the "Equatorial Group" of telescopes (Dome A, B, C, D, E, F) and the 100 inch (254 cm) aperture [Isaac Newton Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton_Telescope "Isaac Newton Telescope"). The institution at Herstmonceux Castle was known as the Royal Greenwich Observatory, where it remained until 1988, when the observatory relocated to Cambridge.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-16)

Today, the domes of the "Equatorial Group" are used as the Observatory Science Centre - a publicly accessible science museum, observatory and planetarium. Dome A houses the 30-inch [Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Henry_Thompson,_1st_Baronet "Sir Henry Thompson, 1st Baronet")[reflecting telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflecting_telescope "Reflecting telescope"), Dome B houses the 36-inch [Yapp reflecting telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yapp_telescope "Yapp telescope"), Dome C houses a 34-inch Hewitt camera, Dome D houses the 13-inch astrographic [refractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractor "Refractor"), Dome E houses the 26-inch [Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Henry_Thompson,_1st_Baronet "Sir Henry Thompson, 1st Baronet") refractor, while Dome F houses the 38-inch [Schmidt telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_telescope "Schmidt telescope"). The largest instrument, the Isaac Newton Telescope, was moved to [La Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Palma "La Palma") in the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands") in the 1970s. The Observatory Science Centre has taken on the maintenance and upkeep of the grade II* listed observatory, which had fallen into disrepair before their tenancy. The empty dome for the Newton Telescope remains on this site and is a landmark, visible from afar.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-17)

### University Study Centre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: University Study Centre")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Herstmonceux_Castle_interior_corridor.jpg/250px-Herstmonceux_Castle_interior_corridor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Interiorcorridor.JPG)

Interior corridor of the castle

In 1992 [Alfred Bader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Bader "Alfred Bader"), an alumnus of [Queen's University at Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_at_Kingston "Queen's University at Kingston"), learned of the castle's vacancy and offered to purchase the castle for his wife; she declined, joking that there would be "too many rooms to clean".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-18) But in 1994, after intensive renovations, the Queen's International Study Centre was opened. It hosts primarily undergraduate students studying arts, science, or commerce through the Canadian University Study Abroad Program (CUSAP), as well as graduate students studying Public International Law or International Business Law. Specialty summer programmes (May–June) including engineering (Global Project Management), archaeology, international health sciences, and law have become popular in recent years with students from both Queen's and other universities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-19) In late January 2009, the ISC was renamed the Bader International Study Centre.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-20) As part of the 25th anniversary celebrations, new science and innovation labs were opened on the campus to increase the ability for first year science-tracked students to attend.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-Silver_celebration_at_The_Castle-21) In 2022, the Bader International Study Centre was renamed Bader College.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-22) On 13 November 2023, in response to engineering investigations, the university suspended operations at Bader College and future admissions to Bader College programs until structural remediation activities can be completed.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-23) Bader College is expected to reopen by 2026.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-24)

### Historical retinue and events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Historical retinue and events")]

Herstmonceux Castle is associated with a retinue of historical re-enactment troops including archers, knights, and falconers, who fly their birds over the grounds.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-Silver_celebration_at_The_Castle-21) The castle is host to a large medieval weekend in August of each year,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-25) and is also hired out for weddings and weekend events.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-26)

### Water lilies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Water lilies")]

In 2025, the [Royal Horticultural Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Horticultural_Society "Royal Horticultural Society") announced that the water lily collection at the castle would be recognised as the National collection for [Nymphaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea "Nymphaea") hardy water lilies.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-27)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

The castle was used for filming part of _[The Silver Chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silver\_Chair "The Silver Chair")_, a 1990 [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") adaptation of the book (one of _[The Chronicles of Narnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Chronicles\_of\_Narnia "The Chronicles of Narnia")_) by [C. S. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._S._Lewis "C. S. Lewis"). The castle and gardens were used by comedians [Reeves and Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_and_Bob "Vic and Bob") for one of their Mulligan and O'Hare sketches. In August 2002, [The Coca-Cola Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Coca-Cola_Company "The Coca-Cola Company") rented the castle for use as part of a prize in a [Harry Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter "Harry Potter")-themed [sweepstakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweepstakes "Sweepstakes")—the castle served as "[Hogwarts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogwarts "Hogwarts")" in a day of Harry Potter-related activities for the sweepstakes winners. A "painting" of the castle was used as a magical cursed object in the U.S. television show _[Charmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charmed "Charmed")_ – episode 2.3 "[The Painted World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Painted_World "The Painted World")".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-28) Due to its suitable appearance, Herstmonceux Castle was a filming location for the series [My Lady Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Lady_Jane "My Lady Jane").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-29)
