**Herstmonceux Castle** is a brick-built [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle"), dating from the 15th century, near [Herstmonceux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux "Herstmonceux"), [East Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Sussex "East Sussex"), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). It is one of the oldest significant brick buildings still standing in England.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) The castle was renowned for being one of the first buildings to use that material in England, built using bricks made from local clay by builders from Flanders.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-2) It dates from 1441.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3) Construction began under the then-owner, [Sir Roger Fiennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fiennes "Roger Fiennes"), and was continued after his death in 1449 by his son, [Lord Dacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Fiennes,_7th_Baron_Dacre "Richard Fiennes, 7th Baron Dacre").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3)

The castle was sold in 1708 to [George Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Naylor "George Naylor"). His descendant, Robert Hare-Naylor, had the interior of the castle demolished in 1776–77 to turn it into a picturesque landscape feature in the grounds of [Herstmonceux Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Place "Herstmonceux Place"). In the early twentieth century, the castle was restored in two separate building campaigns for Colonel [Claude Lowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lowther "Claude Lowther") and [Sir Paul Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Paul_Latham,_2nd_Baronet "Sir Paul Latham, 2nd Baronet"). Herstmonceux was gifted to [Queen's University at Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_at_Kingston "Queen's University at Kingston"), a Canadian university, in 1993 by Alfred and Isabel Bader.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-5)

The parks and gardens of Herstmonceux Castle and Place are Grade II* listed on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLECastle-3) Other listed structures on the Herstmonceux estate include the Grade II listed walled garden to the north of the castle,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLEWallGarden-6) and the Grade II* listed telescopes and workshops of the Herstmonceux Science Centre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-NHLEScience-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early history")]

The first written evidence of the existence of the Herst settlement appears in [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror")'s [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book") of 1086, which reports that one of William's closest supporters granted tenancy of the manor at Herst to a man named 'Wilbert'.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1) By the end of the twelfth century, the family at the manor house at Herst had considerable status. Written accounts mention a lady called Idonea de Herst, who married a Norman nobleman named Ingelram de Monceux. Around this time, the manor began to be called the "Herst of the Monceux", a name that eventually became Herstmonceux.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-:0-1)

A descendant of the Monceux family, [Roger Fiennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fiennes "Roger Fiennes"), was ultimately responsible for the construction of Herstmonceux Castle in the County of Sussex. Sir Roger was appointed Treasurer of the Household of [Henry VI of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VI_of_England "Henry VI of England") and needed a house fitting a man of his position, so construction of the castle on the site of the old manor house began in 1441. It was this position as treasurer which enabled him to afford the £3,800 construction of the original castle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-8)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg/250px-Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hurstmonceux_floorplan.jpg)

Floor plan of the original house; (l) ground floor, (r) first floor

In 1541, Sir Thomas Fiennes, Lord Dacre, was tried for murder and robbery of the King's deer after his poaching exploits on a neighboring estate resulted in the death of a gamekeeper. He was convicted and hanged as a [commoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commoner "Commoner"), and the Herstmonceux estate was temporarily confiscated by [Henry VIII of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England"), but was restored to the Fiennes family during the reign of one of Henry's children.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-9)

The profligacy of the 15th [Baron Dacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Dacre "Baron Dacre"), heir to the Fiennes family, forced him to sell in 1708 to [George Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Naylor "George Naylor"), a lawyer of [Lincoln's Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln's_Inn "Lincoln's Inn") in London. Bethaia Naylor, who became the heiress of Herstmonceux on the death of her brother's only daughter, married [Francis Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Hare_(bishop) "Francis Hare (bishop)") and produced a son, Francis, who inherited in turn, his mother's property. The castle eventually came into the possession of [Robert Hare-Naylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Hare-Naylor "Francis Hare-Naylor"), who, upon the insistence of his second wife, Henrietta Henckell, followed the architect [Samuel Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wyatt "Samuel Wyatt")'s advice to reduce the Castle to a picturesque ruin by demolishing the interior.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-10) Thomas Lennard, 17th Baron Dacre, was sufficiently exercised as to commission [James Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lambert_(painter) "James Lambert (painter)") of Lewes to record the building in 1776.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-12) The castle was dismantled in 1777 leaving the exterior walls standing and remained a ruin until the early 20th century.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-13)

### 20th-century restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 20th-century restoration")]

Radical restoration work was undertaken by Colonel [Claude Lowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lowther "Claude Lowther") in 1913 to transform the ruined building into a residence and, based on a design by the architect, [Walter Godfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Godfrey_(architect) "Walter Godfrey (architect)"), this work was completed by [Sir Paul Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Paul_Latham,_2nd_Baronet "Sir Paul Latham, 2nd Baronet") in 1933. The existing interiors largely date from that period, incorporating architectural antiques from England and France. The one major change in planning was the combination of the four internal [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") into one large one. The restoration work, regarded as the apex of Godfrey's architectural achievement, was described by the critic [Sir Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner") as executed 'exemplarily'.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-14)

### Royal Greenwich Observatory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Royal Greenwich Observatory")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg/250px-Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herstmonceux_Observatory_aerial_view.jpg)

Aerial view of the former Royal Greenwich Observatory at Herstmonceux; the six domes of the "Equatorial Group" of telescopes can be seen to the left, the former location of the [Isaac Newton Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton_Telescope "Isaac Newton Telescope") is the single dome to the right

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Royal_Greenwich_Observatory%2C_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg/250px-Royal_Greenwich_Observatory%2C_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Royal_Greenwich_Observatory,_Herstmonceux_-_April_2012.jpg)

The former Royal Greenwich Observatory at Herstmonceux

The [Royal Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Observatory,_Greenwich "Royal Observatory, Greenwich") was founded by King Charles II at [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich") in 1675.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-15) Observing conditions at Greenwich deteriorated following the urban growth of London, and plans were made in the early 20th century to relocate the observatory to a rural location with clearer, darker skies. Herstmonceux Castle and estate were put up for sale by their private owners and were sold in 1946 to the [Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Admiralty "British Admiralty"), which then operated the Royal Observatory on behalf of the British government. The relocation of the observatory took place over a decade, and was complete by 1957. A number of new buildings were erected in the castle grounds, most notably the domes of the "Equatorial Group" of telescopes (Dome A, B, C, D, E, F) and the 100 inch (254 cm) aperture [Isaac Newton Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton_Telescope "Isaac Newton Telescope"). The institution at Herstmonceux Castle was known as the Royal Greenwich Observatory, where it remained until 1988, when the observatory relocated to Cambridge.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-16)

Today, the domes of the "Equatorial Group" are used as the Observatory Science Centre - a publicly accessible science museum, observatory and planetarium. Dome A houses the 30-inch [Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Henry_Thompson,_1st_Baronet "Sir Henry Thompson, 1st Baronet")[reflecting telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflecting_telescope "Reflecting telescope"), Dome B houses the 36-inch [Yapp reflecting telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yapp_telescope "Yapp telescope"), Dome C houses a 34-inch Hewitt camera, Dome D houses the 13-inch astrographic [refractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractor "Refractor"), Dome E houses the 26-inch [Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Henry_Thompson,_1st_Baronet "Sir Henry Thompson, 1st Baronet") refractor, while Dome F houses the 38-inch [Schmidt telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_telescope "Schmidt telescope"). The largest instrument, the Isaac Newton Telescope, was moved to [La Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Palma "La Palma") in the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands") in the 1970s. The Observatory Science Centre has taken on the maintenance and upkeep of the grade II* listed observatory, which had fallen into disrepair before their tenancy. The empty dome for the Newton Telescope remains on this site and is a landmark, visible from afar.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-17)

### University Study Centre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: University Study Centre")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Herstmonceux_Castle_interior_corridor.jpg/250px-Herstmonceux_Castle_interior_corridor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Interiorcorridor.JPG)

Interior corridor of the castle

In 1992 [Alfred Bader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Bader "Alfred Bader"), an alumnus of [Queen's University at Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_at_Kingston "Queen's University at Kingston"), learned of the castle's vacancy and offered to purchase the castle for his wife; she declined, joking that there would be "too many rooms to clean".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-18) But in 1994, after intensive renovations, the Queen's International Study Centre was opened. It hosts primarily undergraduate students studying arts, science, or commerce through the Canadian University Study Abroad Program (CUSAP), as well as graduate students studying Public International Law or International Business Law. Specialty summer programmes (May–June) including engineering (Global Project Management), archaeology, international health sciences, and law have become popular in recent years with students from both Queen's and other universities.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-19) In late January 2009, the ISC was renamed the Bader International Study Centre.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-20) As part of the 25th anniversary celebrations, new science and innovation labs were opened on the campus to increase the ability for first year science-tracked students to attend.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-Silver_celebration_at_The_Castle-21) In 2022, the Bader International Study Centre was renamed Bader College.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-22) On 13 November 2023, in response to engineering investigations, the university suspended operations at Bader College and future admissions to Bader College programs until structural remediation activities can be completed.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-23) Bader College is expected to reopen by 2026.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-24)

### Historical retinue and events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Historical retinue and events")]

Herstmonceux Castle is associated with a retinue of historical re-enactment troops including archers, knights, and falconers, who fly their birds over the grounds.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-Silver_celebration_at_The_Castle-21) The castle is host to a large medieval weekend in August of each year,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-25) and is also hired out for weddings and weekend events.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-26)

### Water lilies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Water lilies")]

In 2025, the [Royal Horticultural Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Horticultural_Society "Royal Horticultural Society") announced that the water lily collection at the castle would be recognised as the National collection for [Nymphaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea "Nymphaea") hardy water lilies.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-27)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herstmonceux_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

The castle was used for filming part of _[The Silver Chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silver\_Chair "The Silver Chair")_, a 1990 [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") adaptation of the book (one of _[The Chronicles of Narnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Chronicles\_of\_Narnia "The Chronicles of Narnia")_) by [C. S. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._S._Lewis "C. S. Lewis"). The castle and gardens were used by comedians [Reeves and Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_and_Bob "Vic and Bob") for one of their Mulligan and O'Hare sketches. In August 2002, [The Coca-Cola Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Coca-Cola_Company "The Coca-Cola Company") rented the castle for use as part of a prize in a [Harry Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter "Harry Potter")-themed [sweepstakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweepstakes "Sweepstakes")—the castle served as "[Hogwarts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogwarts "Hogwarts")" in a day of Harry Potter-related activities for the sweepstakes winners. A "painting" of the castle was used as a magical cursed object in the U.S. television show _[Charmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charmed "Charmed")_ – episode 2.3 "[The Painted World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Painted_World "The Painted World")".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-28) Due to its suitable appearance, Herstmonceux Castle was a filming location for the series [My Lady Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Lady_Jane "My Lady Jane").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herstmonceux_Castle#cite_note-29)

**Bishop's Castle** is a [market town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") in the south west of [Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire"), England. According to the 2011 Census it had a population of 1,893.

Bishop's Castle is 1.5 miles (2.4 km) east of the [Wales–England border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales%E2%80%93England_border "Wales–England border"), about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of [Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow "Ludlow") and about 20 miles (30 km) south-west of [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury"). To the south is [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun") and to the east is [Church Stretton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Stretton "Church Stretton"). The town is within an agricultural area and has also become known for its alternative community including artists, musicians, writers and craftspeople. The surrounding area is [hillwalking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillwalking "Hillwalking") country and Bishop's Castle is a "Walkers are Welcome Town", gaining the award in 2008. The [long distance footpath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_distance_footpath "Long distance footpath") the [Shropshire Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Way "Shropshire Way") runs through the town and [Offa's Dyke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offa's_Dyke "Offa's Dyke") is only a few miles to the west.

The [ancient trackway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_trackway "Ancient trackway") of the Kerry Ridgeway, a [prehistoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric "Prehistoric")[Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") route, runs from the town. The BC Ring, a 60-mile (100 km) challenging route around the town, was published in 2008. The town has two [micro-breweries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-breweries "Micro-breweries"), including the [Three Tuns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tuns_Brewery "Three Tuns Brewery"), the UK's oldest brewery.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### The castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The castle")]

Documented history begins in [Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") times for Bishop's Castle when Edwin Shakehead, grateful for being miraculously cured of the palsy at [Saint Ethelbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht_II_of_East_Anglia "Æthelberht II of East Anglia")'s tomb in [Hereford Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereford_Cathedral "Hereford Cathedral") gave part of his lands to the incumbent [Bishop of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Hereford "Bishop of Hereford"). A later Bishop of Hereford built a castle, originally a [motte and bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motte_and_bailey "Motte and bailey") design, in 1087 to defend the church and village from the threat of the [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_people "Welsh people") (its site [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid")[SO323891](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/332300_289100_115)). The castle has been under attack several times, not always by Welsh raiders, most notably in 1263 when [John Fitzalan, Lord of Arundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fitzalan_(1246-1272) "John Fitzalan (1246-1272)") and feudal Lord of [Oswestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswestry "Oswestry") and [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun"), held it under siege in the course of a feud with the Bishop of Hereford and caused significant damage, estimated at 1,060 [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_(money) "Mark (money)").

In the Early Middle Ages the castle and parish were situated partly in Wales and partly in England so territorial disputes literally 'came with the territory'.

In 1557 the castle was described as follows: "thirteen rooms covered with lead, a tower on the outer wall on the eastern side containing a stable, and two rooms covered with tiles. There were two other rooms called 'le new buyldinge' situated on the outer wall between the building over the gate and the tower called 'le prison tower'. There was also a dovecote, a garden, a forest and a park."[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

As peace came to the [Welsh Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Marches "Welsh Marches") Bishop's Castle became one of the notorious [rotten boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_boroughs "Rotten boroughs"), an electorally corrupt situation wherein the tiny borough elected two members of parliament from 1585.

In 1618 the castle started to deteriorate and in the 1700s the stone keep and surroundings were flattened to make a bowling green. (Some historians believe that the houses along Market Square and Castle Street were built upon the foundations of an outer wall due to the curvature of the houses).

In 1642, the [Three Tuns Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tuns_Brewery "Three Tuns Brewery") was established on its current site, making it the oldest licensed brewery site in Britain. While some of the current building dates to the seventeenth century, the main building is a Victorian tower brewery erected about 1888.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-2)

In 1719 – the fifth year of the reign of [George I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Great_Britain "George I of Great Britain") and the year [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") published [Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe") – the Castle Hotel was constructed over the site of the old _baille_ [the French word for an enclosed court] of the ancient castle. It was built on the orders of a local landowner, [James Brydges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brydges,_1st_Duke_of_Chandos "James Brydges, 1st Duke of Chandos") (1673–1744), who in the year the hotel was completed was created Duke of Chandos. In an age of unabashed corruption, he acquired a number of lucrative sinecure offices and amassed such wealth that he was known as 'Princely Chandos'.

The 1st Duke of Chandos sold the Castle Hotel to John Walcot who in turn sold it to [Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive of Plassey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Clive,_1st_Baron_Clive_of_Plassey "Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive of Plassey") (1725–1774), known as 'Clive of India', who amassed such wealth during his time in that country that [Horace Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Walpole "Horace Walpole") writing from London to a country friend said: 'you will be frightened by the dearness of everything ... I expect that a pint of milk will soon not be sold under a diamond, and then nobody can keep a cow but my Lord Clive'.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] From Lord Clive the hotel descended to his son, [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Clive,_1st_Earl_of_Powis "Edward Clive, 1st Earl of Powis"), and then to his [grandson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Powis "Edward Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis"), who changed the family name to Herbert, his mother's maiden name. The older Edward became [Earl of Powis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Powis "Earl of Powis") on the death of his brother-in-law, [George Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Powis "George Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis") (of the previous creation of that title).

Local landowners, including Lord Clive, expended large sums of cash buying votes, a common practice at the time in some areas to ensure a seat in Parliament. In 1726 one unsuccessful parliamentary candidate was subsequently able to prove that of the 52 people voting for his rival, the incumbent MP, 51 had received bribes and inducements. The [Reform Act 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") eradicated this practice and Bishop's Castle was disenfranchised.

All that is physically left of the castle today is a 10 metres (30 feet) long, coursed stone wall on the west side of the castle site which is 2 metres (6 feet) thick and 3 metres (10 feet) high. It was overgrown with ivy and was recently renovated to keep it safe and stable. The Castle Hotel stands on the site of the castle itself and is largely built of stone salvaged from the original castle.

### The town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The town")]

The layout of the town in the present day shows that originally the town was made up of 46 [burgage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgage "Burgage") plots which were separated by a few small lanes which have developed to be Church Street, Union Street and Station Street.

In 1249 a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") for a weekly market and an annual fair was granted. They are both still very popular.

In the 17th century, [Bishop's Castle Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_Town_Hall "Bishop's Castle Town Hall") was constructed as a new administrative centre, a court and a prison. It was refurbished with support from the [Heritage Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund") and was re-opened in June 2014.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-3)

The town was classified as a [municipal borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_borough "Municipal borough") in 1885. It lost this status in the 1960s, but still has a mayor and its regalia. It is now a "Quality Town Council".

Bishop's Castle was close to the epicentre of a magnitude 5.1 [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Bishop's_Castle_earthquake "1990 Bishop's Castle earthquake") on 2 April 1990, which was felt throughout much of England and Wales.

The town is located close to the [Shropshire Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Hills_Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty "Shropshire Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty").

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Governance")]

From 1584 to 1832 it was [its own parliamentary borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bishop's Castle (UK Parliament constituency)") with two MPs. It was part of the [Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Ludlow (UK Parliament constituency)") constituency from 1885 until its redesignation as [South Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shropshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "South Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)") in 2024 following constituency boundary changes.

Today the town forms a [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_England "Civil parishes in England"), with its own [town council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_council "Town council") and mayor. The original Town Council website was one of the first in the UK to publish agendas and minutes (from late 2000).

An [electoral ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wards_and_electoral_divisions_of_the_United_Kingdom "Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom") of the same name exists in the [Shropshire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Council "Shropshire Council"). This ward stretches north east to [Ratlinghope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratlinghope "Ratlinghope") and at the 2011 Census had a total population of 3,728.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-4)

## Amenities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Amenities")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Six_Bells_pub_and_brewery%2C_Bishops_Castle%2C_Shropshire.JPG/250px-Six_Bells_pub_and_brewery%2C_Bishops_Castle%2C_Shropshire.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Six_Bells_pub_and_brewery,_Bishops_Castle,_Shropshire.JPG)

Six Bells pub and brewery

There are a variety of shops, local businesses and services ranging from clothes shops to the usual high street banks. The town is notable for a thriving selection of specialist retailers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-5)

There are several [public houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_house "Public house") in the town, and one [micro-brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-brewery "Micro-brewery"): the Three Tuns Brewery.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-6) Additionally, the town sports a number of restaurants and [bed and breakfasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bed_and_breakfast "Bed and breakfast"), and a hotel, The Castle Hotel, built on the site of the outer bailey of the old bishop's castle. Other sights in the town include the House on Crutches Museum of country life, the Rail & Transport Museum, and the old cattle market in the centre of town.

Many properties are painted in various colourful hues of blue, pink, yellow and green which are reflected on the Wintles, a new neighbourhood of energy efficient eco-houses built by [Living Villages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_Villages "Living Villages").

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education")]

The town possesses a high school ([Bishop's Castle Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_Community_College "Bishop's Castle Community College")) which teaches 11- to 16-year-olds, around 450 students from the town and surrounding villages and towns. It also has a primary school and a Nursery.

## Sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sport")]

Sports played by local clubs include:

### Cricket

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Cricket")]

Bishop Castle Cricket Club's 1st XI play in Division 2 of the [Shropshire Cricket League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Cricket_League "Shropshire Cricket League"), and the club play friendlies on Sundays, with regular youth coaching sessions (usually Monday evenings) and matches for school age children. Cricket was first recorded being played in 1841 on Love Lane, and the club was officially formed in 1896 at a meeting held in the Six Bells public house, and have played at the Manor Ground since 1946. The 1st XI equalled their highest ever finish of 4th in 2011 (previously achieved in 2009) with a record points total of 332. The club's social base is the Castle Hotel off Market Square.

### Football

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Football")]

Main article: [Bishops Castle Town F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Town_F.C. "Bishops Castle Town F.C.")

[Bishops Castle Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Town_F.C. "Bishops Castle Town F.C.") play in the Montgomeryshire Amateur League and were Division 1 Champions in 2017–18, having previously played for 6 years in the Mercian Regional Football League Division One. Previously they played in Division 1 of the Montgomeryshire Amateur League, having gained promotion from Division 2 in the early 1990s, and having joined Division 2 in 1984–85. Before that they played in various leagues including the South Shropshire League and the West Shropshire Alliance. The club was formed in the 1880s. The club's social base after matches and for meetings is The Kings Head Public House in Church Street. The club play their Home matches at the Community College ground on Colebatch Road.

### Rugby

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Rugby")]

Bishop's Castle and Onny Valley Rugby Club was formed in the late 1970s and spent the early years playing friendly games against teams from Mid-Wales and Shropshire, before joining the league structure in the early 1990s. Now they play in Midlands Division Fourth North.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Transport")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg/250px-Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg)

Minsterley Motors E200 at [Lydham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydham "Lydham"), en route to Bishop's Castle on route 553

Bishop's Castle has been on a main route for travellers since prehistoric times, although the town was bypassed in the 19th century by [Thomas Telford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Telford "Thomas Telford")'s great road. The inns would have provided accommodation for travellers and have stabled their horses.

There is no main road running through the town, though the [A488](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A488_road "A488 road") runs north–south just to the east of the town, on its way from [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury"), [Pontesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontesbury "Pontesbury") and [Minsterley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minsterley "Minsterley") to [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun") and [Knighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knighton,_Powys "Knighton, Powys"). The B4385 runs around the town and connects with the A488.

Bishop's Castle had a railway, the [Bishops Castle Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Railway "Bishops Castle Railway"), between 1865 and 1935. Originally it was meant to go from [Craven Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craven_Arms "Craven Arms") to [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery,_Powys "Montgomery, Powys"), but that speculation failed due to lack of finance. Sections of the old railway can still be seen today, including some of the embankments, bridges and stations. Today the nearest station is [Broome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broome_railway_station "Broome railway station") on the [Heart of Wales Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Wales_Line "Heart of Wales Line").

There is a limited daytime bus service 553 on Mondays to Saturdays between Bishop's Castle and Shrewsbury, operated by local independent operator [Minsterley Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minsterley_Motors "Minsterley Motors").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-11)

**Bishop's Castle** is a [market town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") in the south west of [Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire"), England. According to the 2011 Census it had a population of 1,893.

Bishop's Castle is 1.5 miles (2.4 km) east of the [Wales–England border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales%E2%80%93England_border "Wales–England border"), about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of [Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow "Ludlow") and about 20 miles (30 km) south-west of [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury"). To the south is [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun") and to the east is [Church Stretton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Stretton "Church Stretton"). The town is within an agricultural area and has also become known for its alternative community including artists, musicians, writers and craftspeople. The surrounding area is [hillwalking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillwalking "Hillwalking") country and Bishop's Castle is a "Walkers are Welcome Town", gaining the award in 2008. The [long distance footpath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_distance_footpath "Long distance footpath") the [Shropshire Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Way "Shropshire Way") runs through the town and [Offa's Dyke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offa's_Dyke "Offa's Dyke") is only a few miles to the west.

The [ancient trackway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_trackway "Ancient trackway") of the Kerry Ridgeway, a [prehistoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric "Prehistoric")[Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") route, runs from the town. The BC Ring, a 60-mile (100 km) challenging route around the town, was published in 2008. The town has two [micro-breweries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-breweries "Micro-breweries"), including the [Three Tuns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tuns_Brewery "Three Tuns Brewery"), the UK's oldest brewery.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### The castle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The castle")]

Documented history begins in [Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") times for Bishop's Castle when Edwin Shakehead, grateful for being miraculously cured of the palsy at [Saint Ethelbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht_II_of_East_Anglia "Æthelberht II of East Anglia")'s tomb in [Hereford Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereford_Cathedral "Hereford Cathedral") gave part of his lands to the incumbent [Bishop of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Hereford "Bishop of Hereford"). A later Bishop of Hereford built a castle, originally a [motte and bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motte_and_bailey "Motte and bailey") design, in 1087 to defend the church and village from the threat of the [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_people "Welsh people") (its site [grid reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Survey_National_Grid "Ordnance Survey National Grid")[SO323891](http://streetmap.co.uk/grid/332300_289100_115)). The castle has been under attack several times, not always by Welsh raiders, most notably in 1263 when [John Fitzalan, Lord of Arundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fitzalan_(1246-1272) "John Fitzalan (1246-1272)") and feudal Lord of [Oswestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswestry "Oswestry") and [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun"), held it under siege in the course of a feud with the Bishop of Hereford and caused significant damage, estimated at 1,060 [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_(money) "Mark (money)").

In the Early Middle Ages the castle and parish were situated partly in Wales and partly in England so territorial disputes literally 'came with the territory'.

In 1557 the castle was described as follows: "thirteen rooms covered with lead, a tower on the outer wall on the eastern side containing a stable, and two rooms covered with tiles. There were two other rooms called 'le new buyldinge' situated on the outer wall between the building over the gate and the tower called 'le prison tower'. There was also a dovecote, a garden, a forest and a park."[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

As peace came to the [Welsh Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Marches "Welsh Marches") Bishop's Castle became one of the notorious [rotten boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_boroughs "Rotten boroughs"), an electorally corrupt situation wherein the tiny borough elected two members of parliament from 1585.

In 1618 the castle started to deteriorate and in the 1700s the stone keep and surroundings were flattened to make a bowling green. (Some historians believe that the houses along Market Square and Castle Street were built upon the foundations of an outer wall due to the curvature of the houses).

In 1642, the [Three Tuns Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tuns_Brewery "Three Tuns Brewery") was established on its current site, making it the oldest licensed brewery site in Britain. While some of the current building dates to the seventeenth century, the main building is a Victorian tower brewery erected about 1888.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-2)

In 1719 – the fifth year of the reign of [George I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Great_Britain "George I of Great Britain") and the year [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") published [Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe") – the Castle Hotel was constructed over the site of the old _baille_ [the French word for an enclosed court] of the ancient castle. It was built on the orders of a local landowner, [James Brydges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brydges,_1st_Duke_of_Chandos "James Brydges, 1st Duke of Chandos") (1673–1744), who in the year the hotel was completed was created Duke of Chandos. In an age of unabashed corruption, he acquired a number of lucrative sinecure offices and amassed such wealth that he was known as 'Princely Chandos'.

The 1st Duke of Chandos sold the Castle Hotel to John Walcot who in turn sold it to [Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive of Plassey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Clive,_1st_Baron_Clive_of_Plassey "Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive of Plassey") (1725–1774), known as 'Clive of India', who amassed such wealth during his time in that country that [Horace Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Walpole "Horace Walpole") writing from London to a country friend said: 'you will be frightened by the dearness of everything ... I expect that a pint of milk will soon not be sold under a diamond, and then nobody can keep a cow but my Lord Clive'.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] From Lord Clive the hotel descended to his son, [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Clive,_1st_Earl_of_Powis "Edward Clive, 1st Earl of Powis"), and then to his [grandson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Powis "Edward Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis"), who changed the family name to Herbert, his mother's maiden name. The older Edward became [Earl of Powis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Powis "Earl of Powis") on the death of his brother-in-law, [George Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Herbert,_2nd_Earl_of_Powis "George Herbert, 2nd Earl of Powis") (of the previous creation of that title).

Local landowners, including Lord Clive, expended large sums of cash buying votes, a common practice at the time in some areas to ensure a seat in Parliament. In 1726 one unsuccessful parliamentary candidate was subsequently able to prove that of the 52 people voting for his rival, the incumbent MP, 51 had received bribes and inducements. The [Reform Act 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") eradicated this practice and Bishop's Castle was disenfranchised.

All that is physically left of the castle today is a 10 metres (30 feet) long, coursed stone wall on the west side of the castle site which is 2 metres (6 feet) thick and 3 metres (10 feet) high. It was overgrown with ivy and was recently renovated to keep it safe and stable. The Castle Hotel stands on the site of the castle itself and is largely built of stone salvaged from the original castle.

### The town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The town")]

The layout of the town in the present day shows that originally the town was made up of 46 [burgage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgage "Burgage") plots which were separated by a few small lanes which have developed to be Church Street, Union Street and Station Street.

In 1249 a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") for a weekly market and an annual fair was granted. They are both still very popular.

In the 17th century, [Bishop's Castle Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_Town_Hall "Bishop's Castle Town Hall") was constructed as a new administrative centre, a court and a prison. It was refurbished with support from the [Heritage Lottery Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund") and was re-opened in June 2014.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-3)

The town was classified as a [municipal borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_borough "Municipal borough") in 1885. It lost this status in the 1960s, but still has a mayor and its regalia. It is now a "Quality Town Council".

Bishop's Castle was close to the epicentre of a magnitude 5.1 [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Bishop's_Castle_earthquake "1990 Bishop's Castle earthquake") on 2 April 1990, which was felt throughout much of England and Wales.

The town is located close to the [Shropshire Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Hills_Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty "Shropshire Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty").

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Governance")]

From 1584 to 1832 it was [its own parliamentary borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bishop's Castle (UK Parliament constituency)") with two MPs. It was part of the [Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Ludlow (UK Parliament constituency)") constituency from 1885 until its redesignation as [South Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shropshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "South Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)") in 2024 following constituency boundary changes.

Today the town forms a [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_England "Civil parishes in England"), with its own [town council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_council "Town council") and mayor. The original Town Council website was one of the first in the UK to publish agendas and minutes (from late 2000).

An [electoral ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wards_and_electoral_divisions_of_the_United_Kingdom "Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom") of the same name exists in the [Shropshire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Council "Shropshire Council"). This ward stretches north east to [Ratlinghope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratlinghope "Ratlinghope") and at the 2011 Census had a total population of 3,728.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-4)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Amenities")]

Six Bells pub and brewery

There are a variety of shops, local businesses and services ranging from clothes shops to the usual high street banks. The town is notable for a thriving selection of specialist retailers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-5)

There are several [public houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_house "Public house") in the town, and one [micro-brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-brewery "Micro-brewery"): the Three Tuns Brewery.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-6) Additionally, the town sports a number of restaurants and [bed and breakfasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bed_and_breakfast "Bed and breakfast"), and a hotel, The Castle Hotel, built on the site of the outer bailey of the old bishop's castle. Other sights in the town include the House on Crutches Museum of country life, the Rail & Transport Museum, and the old cattle market in the centre of town.

Many properties are painted in various colourful hues of blue, pink, yellow and green which are reflected on the Wintles, a new neighbourhood of energy efficient eco-houses built by [Living Villages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_Villages "Living Villages").

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education")]

The town possesses a high school ([Bishop's Castle Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle_Community_College "Bishop's Castle Community College")) which teaches 11- to 16-year-olds, around 450 students from the town and surrounding villages and towns. It also has a primary school and a Nursery.

## Sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sport")]

Sports played by local clubs include:

### Cricket

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Cricket")]

Bishop Castle Cricket Club's 1st XI play in Division 2 of the [Shropshire Cricket League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Cricket_League "Shropshire Cricket League"), and the club play friendlies on Sundays, with regular youth coaching sessions (usually Monday evenings) and matches for school age children. Cricket was first recorded being played in 1841 on Love Lane, and the club was officially formed in 1896 at a meeting held in the Six Bells public house, and have played at the Manor Ground since 1946. The 1st XI equalled their highest ever finish of 4th in 2011 (previously achieved in 2009) with a record points total of 332. The club's social base is the Castle Hotel off Market Square.

### Football

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Football")]

Main article: [Bishops Castle Town F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Town_F.C. "Bishops Castle Town F.C.")

[Bishops Castle Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Town_F.C. "Bishops Castle Town F.C.") play in the Montgomeryshire Amateur League and were Division 1 Champions in 2017–18, having previously played for 6 years in the Mercian Regional Football League Division One. Previously they played in Division 1 of the Montgomeryshire Amateur League, having gained promotion from Division 2 in the early 1990s, and having joined Division 2 in 1984–85. Before that they played in various leagues including the South Shropshire League and the West Shropshire Alliance. The club was formed in the 1880s. The club's social base after matches and for meetings is The Kings Head Public House in Church Street. The club play their Home matches at the Community College ground on Colebatch Road.

### Rugby

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Rugby")]

Bishop's Castle and Onny Valley Rugby Club was formed in the late 1970s and spent the early years playing friendly games against teams from Mid-Wales and Shropshire, before joining the league structure in the early 1990s. Now they play in Midlands Division Fourth North.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bishop%27s_Castle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Transport")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg/250px-Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minsterley_E200_at_Lydham.jpg)

Minsterley Motors E200 at [Lydham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydham "Lydham"), en route to Bishop's Castle on route 553

Bishop's Castle has been on a main route for travellers since prehistoric times, although the town was bypassed in the 19th century by [Thomas Telford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Telford "Thomas Telford")'s great road. The inns would have provided accommodation for travellers and have stabled their horses.

There is no main road running through the town, though the [A488](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A488_road "A488 road") runs north–south just to the east of the town, on its way from [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury"), [Pontesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontesbury "Pontesbury") and [Minsterley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minsterley "Minsterley") to [Clun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clun "Clun") and [Knighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knighton,_Powys "Knighton, Powys"). The B4385 runs around the town and connects with the A488.

Bishop's Castle had a railway, the [Bishops Castle Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Castle_Railway "Bishops Castle Railway"), between 1865 and 1935. Originally it was meant to go from [Craven Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craven_Arms "Craven Arms") to [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery,_Powys "Montgomery, Powys"), but that speculation failed due to lack of finance. Sections of the old railway can still be seen today, including some of the embankments, bridges and stations. Today the nearest station is [Broome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broome_railway_station "Broome railway station") on the [Heart of Wales Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Wales_Line "Heart of Wales Line").

There is a limited daytime bus service 553 on Mondays to Saturdays between Bishop's Castle and Shrewsbury, operated by local independent operator [Minsterley Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minsterley_Motors "Minsterley Motors").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle#cite_note-11)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Museum in Lancaster, England

[![Image 4: Logo comprising the museum's name and the constabulary's badge](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/a/ab/Logo_of_Lancashire_Police_Museum.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Logo_of_Lancashire_Police_Museum.png)

**Lancashire Police Museum** is the museum of the [Lancashire Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Constabulary "Lancashire Constabulary"), in [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Lancashire "Lancaster, Lancashire"), England. It is housed within Lancaster Castle in A Wing of the former [HM Prison Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Prison_Lancaster "HM Prison Lancaster"), and opened in June 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-blade-1) It comprises 16 displays, shown in the former prison cells.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-about-2)

The museum welcomed its 40,000th visitor in May 2024,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-deamer-3) and won a Judges' Commendation in the 2024 Lancashire Tourism Awards, in the "Small visitor attraction" category.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-blade-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Museum in Lancaster, England

[![Image 4: Logo comprising the museum's name and the constabulary's badge](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/a/ab/Logo_of_Lancashire_Police_Museum.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Logo_of_Lancashire_Police_Museum.png)

**Lancashire Police Museum** is the museum of the [Lancashire Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Constabulary "Lancashire Constabulary"), in [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Lancashire "Lancaster, Lancashire"), England. It is housed within Lancaster Castle in A Wing of the former [HM Prison Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Prison_Lancaster "HM Prison Lancaster"), and opened in June 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-blade-1) It comprises 16 displays, shown in the former prison cells.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-about-2)

The museum welcomed its 40,000th visitor in May 2024,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-deamer-3) and won a Judges' Commendation in the 2024 Lancashire Tourism Awards, in the "Small visitor attraction" category.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Police_Museum#cite_note-blade-1)
